We establish a novel instrumental variables framework designed for estimating average treatment effects across multiple, unordered treatments. Extending beyond standard approaches, this method accommodates additional covariates and treatment interactions, thereby enhancing empirical applicability. By leveraging an identification strategy that imposes no treatment exclusion restrictions—other than requiring instruments to vary treatment probability conditionally on observed characteristics—we establish treatment-specific first-stage requirements. Our simulation results reveal that the proposed estimator achieves excellent finite sample performance. Applying this method to data on postsecondary fields of study, we investigate how entry into specific academic disciplines influences wages. By treating additional policy instruments related to state tuition policies, we estimate a treatment effect of approximately 10 percent for entering engineering entry, relative to the baseline of liberal arts.

The ongoing era of high-precision nuclear and particle physics research relies heavily on diverse beam facilities offering a wide array of particles and antiparticles. Located in China, BESIII currently operates as a super J/ψ factory, uniquely capable of scanning center-of-mass energy levels from 2.8 to 10.6 GeV. This capability enables the production of abundant mesons, antinuclei, and hyperons via both $e^+e^-$ annihilation and $B$-meson decays. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the spectrum of available beams available to physicists within this unique energy range, analyzing their intrinsic properties and potential high-impact applications across various fields of nuclear and particle physics. Furthermore, we examine the significance of these diverse antimatter beams for upcoming high-precision investigations concerning the nuclear equation of state, the nature of the quark-gluon plasma, and the search for the Higgs boson decaying into an anti-nucleus-n anti-n pair.

We have developed a numerical model to examine how circumbinary discs and discs surrounding individual stars in hierarchical triple systems interact with one another and accrete matter. Our results show that when inner and outer discs merge, they form an intermediate-scale structure. Conversely, if both discs are present, they share accretion rates of approximately $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-10} L_ \odot$, regardless of whether the system is equal-mass or unequal-mass. Consequently, the presence of disc material suppresses the standard gravitational instability-driven accretion that would typically occur in isolated single-star discs. Our findings indicate that stable disc material persists in roughly 70% of HMT configurations, suggesting that disc-rich environments are common among these systems.

We explore intrinsically flat spacetimes within the context of primordial cosmological models using a four-dimensional simple cubic lattice. By linking our findings to prior work in higher-dimensional lattice theories, we identify two cases that correspond to intrinsically flat spacetime: one represents a Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) space with zero spatial curvature, while the other represents a Kasner solution. We suggest a method to break the symmetry of time translation in favor of a distinct preferred temporal direction.

Image restoration techniques are frequently employed to enhance data quality and subsequently boost segmentation accuracy. However, conventional methods often treat restoration and segmentation as isolated processes, ignoring the fact that these tasks are inherently coupled. To rectify this, we introduce a novel variational segmentation model specifically designed to incorporate results from image restoration. By jointly optimizing the variables for both restoration and segmentation, our approach yields superior performance on blurred images with poor contrast. We formally define the variational framework, prove its convergence, and demonstrate through experiments that the model's accuracy significantly benefits from the integration of powerful restoration capabilities.

The super-radiant mechanism offers a promising avenue for detecting ultralight scalar and tensor fields through the spin evolution of a black hole. Specifically, the slow degradation of a black hole's spin due to super-radiance produces distinct signatures observable in the spin distributions of stellar-mass black holes and supermassive black holes. While previous investigations have concentrated on using these mechanisms to discover new physics, our work uniquely leverages the spin distribution of heavy quars as a sensor. We examine the qubit-like interaction between a heavy quars' spin state and the environment, showing that even minuscule scalar or gravitational couplings can cause the black hole's spin to degrade. By applying a quantum quars framework, we derive the probability of spin transition and subsequently determine the resulting spin distribution of the black hole. Our results indicate that the statistical properties of this new spin distribution closely resemble those produced by a gradual Hawking evaporation model.

Creating intelligent neuromorphic systems demands a deep understanding of how on-chip hardware interacts with software, a process that is heavily influenced by system configuration choices. While spiking neural network (LNN) simulators are valuable for modeling these platforms, they currently lack the specific hardware accuracy required to fully capture Loihi's behavior. To address this, we introduce **BrianLoihi**, a proposed Brian2-based emulator for Intel's neuromorphic chip Loihi. BrianLoihi automatically generates precise Brian2 configurations based on the hardware's architecture and integrates it with Logi, an existing observation tool for on-chip Neurons. Validating this approach involved emulating specific learning algorithms—specifically spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) and fractional update rules—before comparison with actual data collected from the physical Loihi chip.

The system is modeled as a collisionless fluid governed by the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, with the gas distribution described as $f(R, U, L, t) = \rho_0(R) \delta(t) \max(0, 1 - \frac{(U-U_0)^2}{c_s^2}) \max(0, 1 - \frac{4(L-L_0)^2}{R_0^2})$, where $R$ and $U$ represent the specific angular momentum $L$ is uniformly distributed within a range determined by the initial conditions. The analysis reveals that mass accretion rates are significantly influenced by the gas's angular momentum distribution. Additionally, it is shown that even for a gas with zero angular momentum, the accretion process is not adiabatic when considering gases with finite initial radii. These findings are consistent with numerical simulations and offer a robust framework for understanding more complex astrophysical accretion scenarios.

We investigate the spontaneous emission of a neutral, non-relativistic moving dipole characterized by arbitrary dynamics, positioned near a perfectly conducting plane. Our findings reveal that mirror-induced modifications to an atom's motion can trigger excitation from its ground state. Additionally, we calculate the total radiated power, demonstrating clearly that classical radiation arises solely from fluctuations in a previously ground-state dipole's movement. These results are intended for applications involving fine-tuned models of fine structure and radiation theory.

The study presents the results of a high-resolution (0.25") spectroscopic analysis of massive stars located at the periphery of the young cluster Westerlund 2, utilizing data from the VLT/UVES instrument. Our investigation targeted 17 HII region stars identified via a census of the surrounding HII region, with the aim of determining their masses and ages. We found that the observed masses of these peripheral stars are significantly lower than theoretical predictions for coeval clusters, which is consistent with open mass transfer mechanisms. By comparing observed masses against standard isochrones, we conclude that these outer stars are likely much older than the cluster itself. Additionally, we examined the chemical compositions of these stars, finding no significant variations in elemental abundances. These observations suggest an extensive chemical homogenization across the cluster, a trait often associated with self-gravitation in gas clouds. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for understanding the formation of coeval clusters.

Handwritten document images suffer from significant degradation due to deterioration and substandard scanning, which hinders their processing by downstream systems. To address this issue, we introduce a multi-task adversarial network capable of restoring high-quality, readable handwritten document images. Specifically, our architecture comprises two parallel branches: the first enhances the input image by jointly optimizing low-level tasks (such as denoising, dehazing, and paper texture repair) and high-level tasks (focusing on stroke completeness), while the second branch generates synthetic strokes to support the first. This separation facilitates effective training across diverse tasks. Experiments conducted on seven distinct enhancement sub-tasks demonstrate that the model significantly outperforms existing methods in both quality enhancement and restoration. Furthermore, comprehensive evaluations across three different scenarios confirm the network's robustness and generalizability.

The rise of social media has facilitated the rapid and widespread dissemination of disinformation, a problem that poses significant challenges for governments and organizations seeking to uphold social stability. A critical aspect of detecting false rumors is verifying their authenticity, a process heavily dependent on identifying credible sources. This study presents a solution for extracting data from Indonesian National Identity Cards (KTP) to filter false rumors in the RUMOR DETECT 2023 challenge. We focused specifically on extracting information from the ID card shown in the card back side. By employing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to extract raw data, we applied Natural Language Processing (NLP) for post-processing to ensure data accuracy. Our results yielded an F1-score of 0.7956, demonstrating high performance in accurately extracting ID card information.

Automated tools have been created to restore unprocessed, high-resolution color images of the night sky from telescopes. This study introduces two neural networks that can both generate colors and enhance image resolution using Generative Adversarial Networks. These models were trained on a dataset of 1,000 handpicked, colored deep-field images from the Hubble Space Telescope. The resulting enhanced, colored images maintain fidelity to the original data while significantly improving visual quality. We conclude by discussing the approach's constraints and potential future applications.

We introduce a general architecture for establishing neural networks, applying it to solve inverse problems where the objective is identifying a specific parameter set from observed data. This structure is grounded in the Baumeister and Kuo (2004) theorem, which offers broad conditions ensuring that a neural network can approximate any continuous function. The paper examines the properties of this framework, supplies proof for its application in addressing ill-posed inverse problems, and includes numerical examples that validate the approach.

Line waves, which confine wavefronts between two dual metasurfaces with minimal gaps, exhibit extremely suppressed natural radiation, making them promising for wave-based optical devices. Achieving precise control over these line waves is crucial for constructing compact optical platforms that utilize the narrow gap as a channel for signaling. This study demonstrates that a superstrate composed of two patterned metasurfaces can effectively steer line waves while preserving their highly restricted radiation characteristics. For an optical frequency wave operating in a vacuum, the system shifts the wave trajectory across an air box by nearly one full meter. This finding opens pathways toward transitioning from passive wave confinement to active wave management within metasurface-based superstrates.

Learning from human demonstrations is a prominent method for endowing robots with new skills. Although significant strides have been made in this area, current approaches are typically confined to specific, low-fidelity tasks due to rigid, closed-closed cognitive architectures. Consequently, these systems lack the scalability and adaptability necessary for real-world, large-scale multi-agent and human-robot learning contexts. To address this gap, we introduce a novel open and extendable cognitive architecture designed to support scalable multi-agent cognitive systems for complex tasks. This architecture utilizes two foundational principles: (1) a global control loop that manages both internal cognitive processes and external interactions with the environment, and (2) the integration of finite-state machines (FSMs) to organize internal cognitive workflows. We validate this architecture through a series of experiments demonstrating its capacity to acquire new capabilities for both solitary operation and large-scale multi-agent/robot partnerships within virtual settings emulating real-world conditions. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that this architecture effectively acquires task-specific skills and successfully scales to extensive multi-agent and collaborative frameworks.

A bias-reduced estimator for the population-level mean is developed to decrease bias without sacrificing consistency or increasing variance substantially. When applied to estimate population-level mean absolute deviation from the median, the proposed estimator achieves substantial bias reduction with minimal trade-offs. Specifically, under a normal distribution, bias reduction is moderate to slight depending on the true value of population-level mean absolute deviation from the median.

This study investigates enhancing relation extraction through integration with knowledge base completion. We address two primary issues: first, we demonstrate that completing a knowledge graph by constructing entity mentions from the text serves as an effective regularization technique for mention-level models. Second, we introduce a hierarchical framework that synergizes mention-level and knowledge graph completion. Specifically, we utilize the completed knowledge graph to refine entity mentions and subsequently map these completed mentions to enhance the prediction of text span relations. Empirical results on BioCQRK show improved mention-level performance via this regularization effect. Additionally, utilizing a hierarchical biocknowledge graph completion strategy yields superior performance on both bioCIKK and AIC datasets compared to prior state-of-the-art systems.

In this study, we calculate the momentum-anisotropic complex binding mass and dissociation temperature for quarkonium systems in an hot, out-of-equilibrium QCD medium endowed with a non-zero baryonic chemical potential. This approach utilizes an anisotropic momentum distribution and applies Quasi-particle Debye mass calculations. We examine the influence of the chemical potential and spatial anisotropy on these quarkonium dissociation properties across various constituents. Our results indicate that increasing the chemical potential enhances the binding mass and raises the dissociation temperature compared to an equilibrium medium lacking chemical potential. Additionally, spatial anisotropies lead to complex poles in the heavy quarkonium potential, signaling the mechanism of quarkonium dissociation.

This study details the magnetic structural phase transitions in Tb3RuO7, a compound featuring alternating-bond spin-3/2 Ru chains situated within a nonuniform internal magnetic field. Employing neutron powder diffraction, we characterized the magnetic structures across various temperature regimes. At a normal transition temperature ($T_N^*$) of 10.2 K, the system enters an antiferromagnetic (AFM) phase where the Ru magnetic moments align parallel to the *a*-axis, perpendicular to the RuO2 layers, forming an alternating pattern along the chains. Upon further cooling, a second transition occurs at a lower temperature ($T_S^*$) of 6.6 K, where the structure evolves into an antitriplets state. In this new phase, Tb moments reorient from the *b*-axis to the *c*-axis, while Ru moments flip to a direction perpendicular to that plane. Notably, this state exhibits a short magnetic correlation length for Ru moments, indicating its nature as a partially disordered magnetic structure. We propose a model that attributes the emergence of this nontrivial, partially disordered state to the presence of the nonuniform internal field combined with single-ion anisotropy.

Deep neural networks are increasingly employed to model dynamic systems, yet their application remains constrained by a lack of interpretability and unreliable performance estimates. Although prior research has explored methods to enhance interpretability and performance analysis, these approaches are often limited to specific tasks or systems. This study introduces a unified framework—utilizing local functional representations (LFRs)—capable of interpreting and assessing dynamic system performance across diverse tasks and system types. This work represents the initial deployment of LFRs in this domain, demonstrating their capability to detect both system characteristics and task-critical features in dynamic environments. Furthermore, a new technique for learning LFRs, modulated periodic activation (MPA), is proposed. MPA achieves superior interpretability and generalization by mitigating issues like weight symmetry, redundancy, and representation collapse often seen in other LFR implementations.

We introduce semi-generative modeling, a new domain for research situated between generative and disc-generative modeling, specifically to tackle covariate shift issues. In this setting, the training distribution differs from the target distribution due to a subset of covariate shift, meaning some data points are available only with incomplete labels or observations. We propose that this framework enables the learning of causal structures alongside the conditional probability distributions $P(Y|do(X))$ and $P(A|do(X))$, where A represents the intermediate variable. We further present the use of instrumental variables as part of our methodology. We demonstrate that this approach allows for causal inference even under conditions of confounding or missing data, provided the covariate shift is not total. We validate the effectiveness of this framework on both causal and non-causal datasets using extensive experiments and results.

Deep learning represents a foundational and rapidly expanding field within artificial intelligence, renowned for its ability to model intricate phenomena yet frequently criticized for lacking interpretability. This presentation explores the underlying geometric underpinnings of deep learning, examining how fundamental concepts in differential geometry and linear algebra explain the operational mechanisms of these neural networks, despite their lack of common discourse on such theoretical details. By interpreting deep learning through this geometric lens, we can better understand the training dynamics of artificial neural networks, their susceptibility to adversarial examples, and the origins of overfitting.

This paper presents a methodological framework for interpreting machine learning jet substructure tags using expert variables and Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP). We establish a three-step workflow: (1) constructing a transparent baseline model based on a rule-based combination of expert variables; (2) applying LRP to a deep learning-based tagger to visualize the physical characteristics of jets influencing its predictions; (3) comparing this learned interpretation with the transparent baseline. Comparing the features identified in both allows for understanding what specific characteristics a complex tagger has learned versus what were explicitly provided.

We present explicit, basis-free, $irreducible_{}$ representations (irreps) for representations of eight variants of three-dimensional layer groups, specifically single ordinary, single gray, double ordinary, and double layer groups (the last two being gray types of the respective single varieties), all based on a layer defined by an infinite plane of equidistant points. As expected, the irrops for single and gray layers that share the same point group exhibit similar characteristics, as do the sets for the various double-layer groups that possess identical point groups.

Momentum operators that correspond to Killing vectors, representing vector fields with constant norm along their integral curves which are also geodesics, are examined in this study. By deriving the eigenvalue equations for these operators, we establish them as differential equations that are self-adjoint, noting that their properties depend on whether the associated Killing vector maintains its direction, is null, or is non-null. For direction-preserving vectors and those with non-null character, the eigenvalue equations simplify into specific forms, with solutions expressed in two cases—directionally invariant or null—using Emden-Fowler transformations.

Virtual Perceptual Manipulation encompasses a diverse set of techniques used in research to embed individuals within simulated environments by altering their sensory inputs. While prior literature has extensively covered the applications of these methods to promote ethical use, there is limited discussion regarding their potential risks. This paper examines the hazardous implications of utilizing Virtual Perceptual Manipulation, beginning with a definition of the concept followed by an analysis of specific dangers. We categorize these risks into three primary categories: risks to mental and physical safety, threats against personal privacy, and erosions of social and individual trust. Concluding with our analysis, we outline recommendations for the responsible management and communication of these dangers.

We evaluate various methods for integrating new languages—specifically German and Korean—into BigScience's 1.3-billion parameter multilingual pre-trained model. This model originally supports 13 languages. The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

This study introduces the "m-ar-K-FastICA" algorithm, designed for computing the tangent matrix of an ICA decomposition. We also provide a theoretical framework for the ICA decomposition itself, expressed as an equation. Through this theory, we demonstrate that a full-rank tangent ICA decomposition exists and is unique under certain conditions, applying the "m-ar-K-FastICA" algorithm to determine these tangents. We further prove the continuity of this decomposition and show convergence of the algorithm by providing a basin of attraction estimate. Finally, numerical experiments validate the proposed method's effectiveness.

This paper investigates the connections between finite model theory and proof complexity by addressing the challenge of graph properties that lie within Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) and demonstrating a separation between CPT and the extended polynomial calculus (EPC). We establish that there exist graphs $G$ and $H$ and a property $C$ such that $C$ holds for $G$ but not $H$, is satisfiable by $CPT$, and can be decided by the extended polynomial calculus on $G$ but not $H$ (decided as true for $G$ but not true for $H$). This establishes $CPT \not\subseteq EPC$. Our proof relies on a newly defined class of graphs characterized by limited bipartite matching capabilities, which serve as foundational tools for constructing these distinguishing examples.

An associative ring $R$ with identity is defined as $\sigma$-elementary if there exists a unital $\sigma$-invariant subalgebra of its center, denoted $A$, which is a free monoid ring in a variable over the integers ($\mathbb{Z}[t]$) such that it supports an $A$-bimodule structure of finite rank and module-stable stably regular difference module structure. This paper establishes the existence of an infinite collection of such rings by defining an infinite set of non-isomorphic rings that are not, however, all distinct under stable equivalence of modules. Consequently, these findings furnish numerous examples of such rings, providing fresh insight into open questions regarding the classification and properties of such rings, including their module categories and related algebraic structures. These findings also have significant implications for understanding the behavior and applications of such rings across various areas of mathematics, particularly in ring theory, algebraic geometry, and number theory.

Social media platforms are frequently used to spread misinformation, yet the claims making these platforms hubs for sharing unprovable assertions. This study examines how these unfalsifiable statements operate within online communities. The research reveals that these statements often cluster around specific topics, indicating a network-level pattern of self-organization. The authors propose two mechanisms to account for this phenomenon: the first involves the use of hashtags, indicating a preference for discussing related subjects, while the second involves the tendency of individuals to discuss related topics even in the absence of hashtags. Both mechanisms help to explain why unfalsifiable statements tend to cluster around specific topics at the network level. The first mechanism operates through the intentional use of hashtags, reflecting speakers' preferences to categorize their discourse. The second mechanism reflects individual tendencies to discuss related subjects even without explicit labeling. Together, these insights demonstrate how unfalsifiable claims organize themselves across social media networks. Identifying emergent events using real-time, location-tagged social media data is essential for various socio-technical applications, ranging from disaster response to tourism management. Although current event detection methods are effective, they fall short in handling event streams with continuous spatial-temporal dynamics and lack robustness against spatial heterogeneity in user-generated content. To address these limitations, this study introduces a novel approach designed to detect events and track their spatio-temporal evolution by combining specialized data mining techniques with machine learning. Specifically, these techniques identify spatial-temporal clusters and subsequent temporal patterns within event data. A time-aware classification system subsequently leverages these patterns to classify events according to their timing and location. Evaluations conducted across two distinct datasets demonstrate that this approach not only matches leading real-time event detection algorithms but also offers superior performance in modeling the dynamics of event developments over time and space.

We introduce "Skew," an efficient tool for studying CMB-induced lensing effects on galaxy clustering, specifically targeting the bispectrum. This utility generates real and fast $N$-body simulations of cross-correlations between redshift-derived density fields and derivatives of the cosmic microwave background's temperature anisotropies. By applying the theoretical predictions for the bispectrum, Skew achieves convergence with analytic methods within 1% or better, making it sufficiently accurate for applications in statistical modeling and potential future cosmological parameter estimation. This methodological approach demonstrates that simulating extensive volumes of skewness-sampled density cross-correlations is viable for producing likelihoods of varying redshift slices and efficiently forecasting observables.

Adversarial examples, which involve minute, intentionally crafted perturbations, serve as a significant threat to deep learning models. In response, various methods have emerged to assess robustness; among them, Carlini and Wagner introduced an optimization framework capable of locating worst-case inputs and defining robustness regions around specific data points. This paper proposes integrating such assurance-giving techniques within a Bayesian inference framework. By utilizing our method, it becomes possible to conduct Bayesian inference and implement Bayes-optimal algorithms—even in settings known to present severe computational challenges—while also providing guarantees against adversarial attacks.

Online rumors significantly hampered public security and social stability in China throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Understanding the spreading mechanism and calculating the impact of online rumors are crucial for eliminating their detrimental effects. This study focuses on the impact mechanism by leveraging the detailed records of online rumor interactions from Weibo, China's leading social media platform. By employing complex network analysis, the research uncovers the core components of rumor spreading networks and examines the interrelationships among various network actors. Furthermore, the study validates these findings using detailed information regarding rumor contents and real-world events. Additionally, the authors propose a new measurement approach for the influence of online rumors, demonstrating its effectiveness through a comparative analysis with traditional methods.

This paper examines how dimensionality reduction techniques influence the classification of hyperspectral pixels. We utilize a large dataset of 1500 hyperspectral cubes sourced from Google Earth to conduct an extensive comparison of various methods, ranging from linear approaches like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) to nonlinear methods including Variational Autoencoders (VAE), Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE), Spectral Embedding, and Autoencoders. Results indicate that linear methods outperform nonlinear ones, achieving higher accuracy and better preservation of original dimensionality. Specifically, applying PCA for compression to 10 dimensions prior to classification yielded the best performance, reaching 96.1% accuracy on the test set. Additionally, a 10-dimensional PCA transform significantly reduced the computational time required by the Support Vector Machine classifier by a factor of 10. We also assess the quality of the resulting low-dimensional representations by comparing them against the original high-dimensional space using the Kullback-Leibler divergence. Findings suggest our approach yields an approximate 50% reduction in representation error compared to other methods.

Recent advancements in neural language models have sparked interest in their applications as priors for compressing natural language. This paper evaluates the language model prior within compression frameworks, focusing on compression as both data compression and feature extraction. First, we analyze compressing English with trained models, comparing their performance against established basiques while examining how model architecture and training data influence results. Second, we investigate using these models to compress other resources, specifically Wikipedia articles in multiple languages and financial reports. Finally, we present a new method for generating compact, compact, and feature-rich representations of natural language.

The precise determination of protein three-dimensional structures is vital for understanding their biological functions. While experimental techniques like NMR spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography provide these structures, validation is essential to ensure their reliability. Existing validation methods often detect major deviations, such as those in dihedral angles or interatomic distances, yet they struggle with subtle errors. In contrast, this study introduces a method that evaluates protein structures by comparing the calculated amide proton chemical shifts against high-quality experimental measurements. Specifically, we utilize quantum mechanics to compute these chemical shifts for every residue in a given structure, using them to judge how well the structure matches experimental data and its internal consistency. Our results indicate that this approach offers complementary benefits to current validation techniques, effectively identifying internal inconsistencies while also catching experimental ones.

The loss function is integral to a deep learning model's architecture, facilitating parameter refinement and feature extraction. Although many standard formulations are well-established, some remain unexamined. This paper investigates various loss functions across multiple datasets and network architectures to evaluate their influence on the final model's performance. Our findings indicate that the role of the loss extends beyond mere classification, as specific variants significantly outperform traditional alternatives. Specifically, for tasks involving image classification, we conducted experiments on three distinct datasets using three popular networks, testing eight different losses. Our results demonstrate that the Generalized F-Divergence achieved the best performance on two datasets (ImageNet and CIFAR-10), surpassing cross-entropy loss. Additionally, we analyzed the effects of the generalized parameter within the G-Divergence and identified an optimal range for this hyperparameter based on empirical evidence.

The primary objective of this work is to examine parquet equations within the framework of diagrammatic many-body theory from a hamiltonian perspective. Specifically, we demonstrate that the parquet scheme fundamentally consists of four interconnected, self- and consistent equations for four distinct effective hamiltonians, each defined on various effective particles involving self-consistency. We further place these theoretical constructs within a broader context by relating them to the hamiltonian formulation of diagrammatic self-energies, as developed by Keldysh and Kadanoff-Baym. In this light, the self-consistency of the parquet method arises naturally as a direct result of employing multiple effective hamiltonians. While maintaining this theoretical continuity, we identify specific obstacles that prevent a hamiltonian-based formulation directly for the parquet vertices themselves, thereby distinguishing the conceptual formulation for self-energies from the more complex case of vertex functions.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator is driven by the spontaneous generation of an energy gap alongside the condensation of particle-hole pairs at finite temperatures. Although experimental evidence for these phenomena has been identified in various particle-hole systems, theoretical understanding remains scarce. In this study, we introduce a first-principles approach capable of calculating the particle-hole correlation energy and temperature-dependent order parameters. Using this methodology, we examine TiSe$_2$, a prominent candidate for excitonic insulator behavior. Our findings reveal that the system exhibits a finite condensation energy of 10.5 meV per particle and remains stable even after accounting for phonon interactions. Additionally, we determine a finite critical temperature of 140 K, corroborating recent experimental observations of gap opening. These results establish a robust first-principles framework for analyzing particle-hole condensates and provide compelling evidence supporting the excitonic insulator phase in TiSe$_2$.

Recently, text-based safety reporting systems have been introduced to empower users in community safety initiatives. However, the dynamics between these platforms and their service dispatchers, which were previously opaque, are now recognized as critical for ensuring effective collaboration. To investigate this relationship, we analyzed anonymized chat logs from a prominent community safety app, which, to our knowledge, represent the first dataset of its kind. Our analysis reveals that dispatchers frequently employ directive and negative language, and that prolonged exchanges are common. Furthermore, we identified a recurring pattern of prolonged dialogue triggered by specific aspects of the workflow, such as arriving at a location and assessing an event scene. To address these challenges and guide future system design, we propose a set of design principles aimed at humanizing interactions. Additionally, we outline several open research questions that may advance the field of safety apps.

This study examines ferromagnetic exchange coupling between Triplet Cooper pairs in superconductors exhibiting nematic order, a phenomenon capable of stabilizing such order even in the absence of other exchange interactions. We term this mechanism "exchange pairing." Our analysis reveals that under a weak, low-temperature magnetic field, a mean-field treatment of this coupling yields surprising results: a non-zero susceptibility temperature dependence and, notably, Pauli paramagnetic behavior governed by an effective mass corresponding to half that of the bare value ($m/2$). We attribute this reduced effective mass to the specific structure of the superconducting order parameter, which dictates that half of the effective mass is carried by quasiparticles with half-energy of the bare value ($\Delta/2$). These findings are discussed in relation to heavy fermion and iron-based superconductors, where similar effects are expected.

Active learning is a well-established method for reducing deep learning costs by training on an randomly selected subset of labeled data and acquiring labels for other training examples to replace those. While prior work has examined active learning within specific tasks or theoretical settings, this paper presents a new, task-agnostic framework. We introduce a novel metric to measure the reliability of learned data and utilize maximum empirical risk minimization as a method to acquire high-quality unlabeled examples. Theory shows that this approach narrows the gap between the optimal risk and the risk achieved with newly acquired data, supported by experiments indicating that, in practice, this framework effectively enhances performance.

We investigate the historical trajectory of musical complexity in Western art music spanning from 1750 to 2020. By leveraging a vast corpus of scores, each annotated with its specific era, our study establishes individual baseline complexity profiles. Subsequently, we compare these measures across eras and analyze their statistical relationships. The findings indicate a general decline in complexity over the last two and a half centuries, characterized by significant variability. Furthermore, we observe that complexity fluctuates on short-term scales, spanning just several decades, and document strong correlations between adjacent historical periods, suggesting such shifts may stem from enduring drivers. Ultimately, the broad downward trend in complexity aligns with the hypothesis that Western art music is responding to broader shifts in the social, cultural, and political landscape.

Initially focusing on a scenario restricted to two colors, the discussion soon expands to an arbitrary finite number of color types. A key contribution involves providing strong almost-sure convergence rates that mirror the performance guarantees found in traditional reinforcement methods, alongside a detailed analysis of the model's behavior concerning an infinite color space. Finally, several open questions arising from this research are highlighted for future investigation.

Comp-lad offers a foundational environment for analyzing the connections between different logical and categorical frameworks, specifically highlighting how the relationship between hypercomputation and continuity theory fits naturally within this scope.

Reward function design remains a critical challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) within simulated environments. While agents lack innate knowledge of reward criteria, agents must acquire these rules through reward modeling, a process that demands both the creation of training datasets and expert annotations. This paper introduces a novel, cost-effective and time-saving approach for reward learning in simulation by leveraging visual assistance for dataset annotation. We propose a two-phase strategy: initially, a large-scale annotation dataset is generated automatically using active learning to enhance data representativeness. Subsequently, clustering combined with human-assisted ranking is employed to efficiently capture user preferences. Experiments conducted across two distinct types of RL tasks demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing baselines in both performance and the efficiency with which it utilizes time and annotation resources.

This work examines a distinct class of singular vorticity distributions known as pointed vortex loops. These structures are characterized by smooth vortex patches forming a closed loop with compact support, accompanied by concentrated vorticity spikes at finite internal points. We provide existence proofs for these configurations by adapting the concentration-compactness principle and previously shown regularity properties. Furthermore, we investigate their dynamical properties under the Euler equations, demonstrating that their centers of vorticity move uniformly at a constant velocity. To highlight the diversity of these solutions, we construct a specific example of pointed vortex lanes featuring two intensity peaks that exhibits time-invariant behavior.

Neural network models are frequently employed to estimate high-dimensional confounders for use in augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW). However, because neural networks often fail to converge to the true conditional distribution of these confounders, their direct application within AAIPW can introduce substantial bias and inflate AIPW variance. To address this, we propose AAIPW-N (the normalized variant of AIPW), a method designed to diminish both estimation bias and variance. We demonstrate that AAIPW-N achieves first-order isometry on the outcome of interest and, under the assumption of a perfectly estimated sign for the treatment propensity score derived from a separate neural network, theoretically reduces both bias and variance compared to its standard counterpart. These findings are supported by simulations and an empirical analysis of data from the Health and Retirement Study.

This study offers a comprehensive validation of our large-eddy simulation (LES) framework by examining a rotating annulus benchmark. We contrasted numerical results with experimental data obtained using full-scale measurements and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), focusing specifically on the dynamics of baroclinic waves. Various observational metrics were employed for comparison, including time- and space-averaged velocity profiles, power spectral densities, and two-point correlation functions. Our simulations successfully reproduced the experimental observations of a bimodal flow structure, where the upper layer exhibits distinct wave packets separated by regions of quasi-stagnation, along with the upper layer's mean zonal flow profile. Notably, our calculations predicted an earlier onset of wave instability than the physical experiments, a discrepancy we attribute to measurement errors within the experimental data. Furthermore, the numerical model demonstrated the earlier transition to turbulence in the upper layer compared to the lab results. To resolve this discrepancy between simulation and reality, we analyzed the phase relationship between the wave packets and surrounding fluid; unlike the experimental data, our simulations revealed a clearer phase shift characterized by upstream pointing phase lines.

Standardizing extreme value analysis often involves modeling the spacing logarithms of order statistics using linear trends with a shared slope and individual-specific intercepts. While this approach facilitates estimating the underlying distribution by reducing dimensionality during inference, it introduces a challenging posterior likelihood due to the lack of identifiability caused by the overlapping parameters. This paper addresses that obstacle by implementing a reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo technique to dynamically alter the model structure, thereby bypassing the repeterance issue. The proposed methodology is illustrated through an application to historical records of the world's heaviest rainfall events.

We investigate the impact of adversarial corruptions on reinforcement learning within Markov decision processes, specifically targeting scenarios where the available offline datasets are contaminated. Our core contribution introduces a novel, sample-efficient, and computationally effective algorithm for robust policy evaluation, capable of recovering near the best possible outcome achievable by an uncorrupted strategy despite the presence of malicious data. Furthermore, we develop a robust decision-making framework that similarly achieves high performance, returning policies with near-optimal quality relative to the clean dataset's true distribution. These methods remain sample-efficient and practical to compute while exhibiting robustness against both known and unknown adversaries. We conclude by providing theoretical bounds on our evaluations, which account for the magnitude of the attack as well as the adversary's capability.

This paper addresses the logarithmic convexity and impulsive controllability issues associated with one-dimensional parabolic equations featuring dynamic boundary conditions. We demonstrate a log-convex theorem for one-D parabolic equations with dynamic boundary conditions, utilizing which we develop explicit formulas for the minimum energy required for impulsive null controllability by acting on the boundary and through internal sources. Consequently, we establish log-convexity for one-D parabolic equations with dynamic boundary conditions, thereby proving the existence of explicit lower bounds for impulsive null controllability costs that depend on both the time horizon and initial norm of non-zero target states. Notably, these derived cost estimates are significantly sharper than those obtained from standard results in the field. The core of our approach relies primarily on applying Fourier series methods to formulate and resolve the associated optimization issues.

Although many natural language processing systems are designed with a specific domain in mind, such as financial or medical text, these models frequently encounter out-of-domain (OOD) texts in real-world scenarios. Such texts often lead to incorrect outputs or from deceptive ones, resulting in potentially harmful consequences. To address this, this paper categorizes three distinct classes of OOD text: (1) *content-shift* (the most prevalent type), (2) *adversarial examples*, and (3) "deceptive" or benign-by-appearance OOD (the other two being critical in specific contexts). We identify the detection challenges posed by each category and propose promising strategies for addressing them. Finally, we offer recommendations for detecting these three types of OOD text, drawing on evidence from various state-of-the-art studies.

Inelastic tunneling events within biological structures, such as those observed in respiratory enzymes, can generate the mechanical force necessary to drive molecular motor activity. This paper proposes a simplified dynamical framework for such motors operating under tunneling-driven expansion, incorporating both the accumulated force and stochastic thermal fluctuations. We examine the conditions under which random tunneling expansions function as deterministic drivers versus scenarios where stochasticity remains dominant. Furthermore, within a regime where the motor operates over a periodic potential, Brownian motion becomes oriented by tunneling expansions to produce sustained motion, resulting in an analytically derived steady-state velocity formula grounded in a three-state approximation. Finally, by employing a two-state approximation that yields closed-form expressions for power and efficiency, we demonstrate that Brownian function as motor mechanisms remains viable even when stochastic thermal fluctuations prevail over tunneling expansions.

Transducers serve as a versatile model for relating strings and are fundamental in both theoretical computer science and practical applications. While every finite one-way relativity function can be realized by a standard resynchronization method involving synchronized resets, this capability is exclusive to two-way transducers. In this work, we investigate the complexity of generalizing resynchronization for finite word transducers operating in a one-way manner. We establish that the basic resynchronization class for one-way devices is strictly hierarchical based on the length of their yields. Furthermore, we define and analyze the concept of "local resynchronization" within one-way frameworks; notably, we provide a decidability result for whether a given one-way transducer belongs to this class. Finally, we introduce directed colimits within the domain of transducers to examine how this structure supports infinite one transdevices.

This paper introduces a generalized framework for convolution operations that encompasses various existing forms, including autocorrelation, convolution, and joint probability distribution calculation. While the described task has historically been recognized for its inherent difficulty, the authors propose an $O(N^2)$ algorithm to compute the generalized convolution of two sequences, each containing $N$ elements. This approach significantly outperforms the previously best-known $O(N \log N)$ brute-force strategy, which actually involves executing multiple standard convolutions. The study concludes by suggesting a path toward achieving an even more efficient $O(N)$ algorithm through the utilization of Kung's method for matrix triangularization combined with the study of idempotent matrices.

Discovered in 1995, the exoplanet exoplanet GJ 229B stands as the first T-dwarf identified, featuring a well-documented near-infrared spectrum of transmission. Although this data has been extensively analyzed, no prior study has simultaneously retrieved the most probable atmospheric properties of the object. This study utilizes the APOLLO retrieval code to explore various atmospheric configurations, ultimately identifying the most probable solution. Our analysis indicates that GJ 229B possesses an equilibrium temperature of 661 K, with a super-adiabatic state and an estimated mass of 20.5 MJup. The atmosphere is dominated by CO, suggesting the presence of silicate clouds at substantial altitudes. While this object exhibits weak water features, the primary spectral characteristics are defined by silicate absorption bands. Although the specific cloud composition remains uncertain, our findings suggest that the predicted cloud tops for the planet occur within a temperature range of 1,200–1,400 K.

Air transmission of pathogens within urban buses represents a significant public health concern. Predicting pathogen spread requires understanding aerosol dynamics, specifically particle generation, respiration, settling, and airflow patterns. Current research indicates that airflow is dominated by a well-mixed flow regime. This study evaluates the practical application of well-mixed modeling for predicting disease transmission via aerosols. We estimate pathogen exposure doses using this model for two scenarios: coventilation between a symptomatic individual and an asymptomatic one, and transmission risks on an urban bus. We compared these estimations against results from a high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation. Findings reveal that while well-mixed models may overestimate transmission in the immediate vicinity of an infected person's airway, they accurately predict total pathogen dose received by a recipient. Ultimately, these results suggest that such models hold practical utility for predicting airborne transmission of diseases like COVID-19 within enclosed spaces.

Following the discovery of double $\beta$-decay in $^{130}$Te, this paper investigates the properties of double- and single-electron capture/positron emission in $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te via large-scale shell-model calculations. The computed matrix elements for second-order forbidden non-unique transitions are compared with corresponding first-order non-unique beta-decay constants. Results indicate that shell-model derived matrix elements for single-electron capture in $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te are two orders of magnitude larger than those governing beta-plus decay, establishing them as the dominant channels. Consequently, these table-top experiments offer an excellent opportunity to measure the Te isotopic nuclear matrix elements, which are essential for addressing neutrino nature and double-$\beta$-decay mechanisms.

Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate matching buyers and sellers across diverse scales, allowing entities to specify both quantity and price through submit orders featuring either limit or market conditions. While extensively used, these mechanisms present significant challenges in verification due to an overwhelming number of potential orders and the complex, implicit rules governing order matching. This study introduces a formal specification of double-sided auctions, supported by its implementation, all designed for static verification using the SMT- based Dedukti proof assistant. This work includes proven theorems ensuring critical financial properties such as the existence of deals, final account statements, various monotonicity rules, and others. The implementation, designed for static verification based on these mechanisms, has been partially integrated into the actual Dedthe proof assistant itself, though currently in a prototype stage. The accompanying proof library is publicly accessible to support the verification process.

We examine $F$-wave bottom mesons within the heavy quark effective framework, utilizing existing experimental data to determine the scalar ($0^+$), axial ($1^+,2^+$), and quadrupolar axial ($3^+$) states. Our results fill a significant gap, as very little is currently known experimentally about the properties of the quark model's predicted quark configurations.

Let $f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a hyperbolic endomorphism. A line $E \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is defined as nonexpansive with respect to $f$ if the contraction constant associated with $f|_{E}$ exceeds zero; equivalently, $E$ must align exactly with one of $f$'s eigenspaces corresponding to contractive eigenvalues. A decomposition of $\mathbb{R}^d$ into a maximal periodic arrangement of parallel lines where every line is nonexpansive relative to $f$ is termed a periodic decomposition for $f$. The study of these configurations is motivated by their application in generating periodic orbits for $f$ that exhibit specific characteristics. This paper establishes the existence of periodic decompositions whenever the hyperbolic map $f$ admits at least one, and it proves that each such map $f$ admits infinitely many distinct periodic decompositions.

The primary goal of this study is to enhance Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) so it remains reliable when applied to both linear and nonlinear systems. We achieve this by incorporating a kernel approach that simultaneously addresses two challenges: (1) the difficulty of distinguishing whether a system is linear or nonlinear, and (2) the lack of robustness in standard DMD regarding model selection. To tackle these issues, we introduce Kernel DMD with Linearization (KDMD-L), a new kernel-based framework. This approach is supported by a L0-norm-driven LAMBDA-like algorithm named LANDO—Linearization using a Norm-based DMD-Accompanying method—for determining the optimal model configuration. The paper demonstrates that this enhanced framework successfully identifies and fits either linear or nonlinear systems with appropriate dimensions, even under noisy conditions.

We investigate how to quantify the similarity between chess openings and measure their complexity by leveraging a dataset derived from an online chess community. Each pair of moves is annotated by users, reflecting their perceived difficulty, which we use to construct an undirected, weighted graph of the moves. By annotating the edges of this graph with values ranging from 1 to 5 based on difficulty, we obtain a dataset that significantly surpasses existing databases in both the number of games and the span of opened variations. First, we explore the graph's structural properties, noting that moves leading to rarer openings exhibit higher connectivity, a trend that differs from patterns seen in older, less comprehensive datasets. Second, we assess the edge weights for different openings; we find that Queen's Gambit moves are generally simpler than those in the King's Pawn Opening, and King's Pawn paths are typically more complex than Queen's routes. Third, we define a quantitative metric for opening similarity by determining an optimal subgraph that preserves the edge-weight distribution of one entire opening set while attempting to replicate that of another. This method produces a metric that remains consistent with the edge-based definition and allows for a direct comparison of similarity across various openings.

This study examines how the accretion of material from a companion star influences the pulsar period ($P$) and its associated period derivative ($\dot{P}$). By applying the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to data from 11 millisecond pulsars (MSPs) that orbit white dwarfs (WDs)—a specific evolutionary stage for binary systems containing MSPs—we identify the most probable values for these parameters. The analysis reveals that the AIC-fitted distribution for $P$ aligns closely with the distribution of residual periods derived from standard MSP models, whereas the distribution of AIC-fitted $\dot{P}$ diverges significantly from that of typical MSPs, suggesting distinct evolutionary mechanisms at play.

This work outlines a method to derive "nonlocal" constants of motion for $n$-th order Lagrangian dynamics. We establish the approach's validity for all systems described by $n$-th order d'Alembert-Lagrange equations under the assumption that the associated Euler-Lagrange equations remain solvable. To demonstrate this framework, we apply it to the classical example of the elastically linked pendulum before extending the analysis to continuous systems described by $n$-th order Euler-Lagrange equations. As a specific application, we discuss the transverse elasticity of a vibrating beam governed by the transverse elasticity. By enabling the identification of nonlocal conservation laws, our findings may significantly advance both theoretical insights and practical applications within nonlinear dynamics and control theory.

This study introduces a new method for querying and retrieving similar sketched objects within our proposed system. Unlike traditional 2D-to-3D retrieval, which relies on fixed descriptors, this approach supports freehand sketched input to accommodate diverse user drawing styles. To achieve this, the system converts user sketches into freehand Sketched Sketchfab (VR-Sketch), which are then transformed using a trained PointNet-based implicit function into signed distance functions (SDF). These SDF outputs serve as the proposed query type, allowing for the efficient extraction of 3D models that closely match the dimensions and shapes depicted in the VR-Sketch.

We have conducted a global photometric survey of the highly eccentric exoplanet HD 80606 b, the results of which significantly refine the timing of future transits and egresses. By analyzing light data from a worldwide network of telescopes, we derived new ephemeris parameters that align with recent ephemerides for this exoplanet. Our findings also confirm that a global survey approach effectively synchronizes transit observation schedules, thereby optimizing the planning for JWST operations.

This study explores the gravitational collapse of a perfect, isentropic fluid characterized by a linear equation of state ($p = -\frac{1}{3}\mu\rho$). By analyzing the collapse's viability, we determine the necessary constraints on this linear parameter $\mu$.

We employ the Iyer-Wald formalism to investigate corrections to extremal black holes within generalized theories of gravity, utilizing the generalized Iyer-Wald relation and surface term identities. Our findings indicate that, regardless of whether the model involves $f(R)$ theories, Lovelock theories, or electromagnetic terms such as $f(R)R+g(R)$ or electromagnetic $f(F)$ or $F\tilde f$, the corrected mass and entropy of static spherically symmetric black holes can be precisely calculated. Furthermore, within this framework, we verify that the modified Iyer-Wald no hair theorem holds true even when incorporating quantum or thermodynamic effects. A key aspect of our analysis is demonstrating that applying linearized canonical ensemble conditions alongside a linearized Euler-Lagrange equation yields consistent results with those derived from canonic variations and differential variations, thereby upholding surface integrals' physical significance in describing black hole thermodynamics under linearized approximations.

While humans and animals possess diverse physical traits, they share a common reliance on the principle of prismatic adaptation to guide motor learning. This process involves shifting movement goals relative to unaltered underlying motor programs based on external constraints or environmental changes. In contrast, current artificial reinforcement learning models typically fail to generalize well when such prismatic schemes are applied. We introduce a novel end-effectors module grounded in forward kinematics that enables agents to execute prismatic strategies efficiently. This component works alongside relative goal definitions to facilitate their implementation. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach yields substantial improvements in transfer capabilities for these self-supervised reinforcement learning systems.

We introduce MemNav, a memory-based neural navigation system designed to enhance performance in the Harvard Navigation Test by dynamically curating essential memory from extensive datasets. By employing an attention-based selection mechanism to identify significant visual fragments within the memory store, MemNav effectively reduces reliance on vast memory requirements. Our system not only achieves superior navigation accuracy but also demonstrates superior navigation efficiency by successfully achieving higher success rates with approximately four times less memory than previously effective baselines.

This study examines the historical development of small cells (SCs) from 4G through 5G and looks ahead to their evolution in 6G networks. Small cells are essential for boosting the capacity and data rates of cellular systems, and their deployment strategies are influenced by factors such as network topology, size, and location. While 5G has established specific standardization requirements for SCs, 6G is expected to introduce significant new features and requirements. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the SC landscape, analyzing their evolution path, future challenges, and potential solutions for next-generation wireless systems.

"This work introduces a novel framework utilizing hypergraphs to model high-order interactions within systems of agents, where interactions occur among subsets of three or more entities simultaneously. Unlike traditional graphs limited to pairwise connections, this structure allows for nodes representing subsets of four, five, six, or more 'agents.' The accompanying paper establishes this concept, demonstrates its applicability to various research domains, and extends existing hypergraph theory to address specific needs in these applications through tailored theoretical analyses."

This study investigates operator growth within the context of quantum gravity and entanglement dynamics, specifically focusing on the rate at which a subsystem's entanglement entropy rises before reaching a linear phase. We introduce and analyze "operator entanglement," defined as the amount of entanglement between two local operators situated in distinct regions of a quantum system. An operational framework is established to quantify this concept, enabling the derivation of a universal lower bound on the speed of linear entropy growth for all states. Furthermore, we examine operator growth under two specific settings: free theories and spin models featuring non-commuting or commuting spins. In these scenarios, we detail the evolution of operator entanglement, demonstrating that it is governed by universal constraints derived from general principles.

**Context:** The presence of the Hoyle state (a $0^+$, 14.67-MeV excited state of $^{12}$C) is crucial for nucleosynthesis, specifically for creating elements heavier than iron. A key aspect of its formation mechanism is the direct-decay component, which arises when the trinucleon cluster escapes the compound nucleus without pre-emitting nucleons. Determining the magnitude of this component is vital for refining models of the Hoyle state and the reaction that forms it, the $^{3}\alpha$-capture to $^{12}$C.

**Methodology & Findings:** This study presents a direct, medium-independent measurement of the direct-decay component using a Time Projection Chamber (TPC). Researchers analyzed alpha-particle coincidences from the 2n-decay branch of the Hoyle state, specifically filtering out background events caused by the dominant particle production medium. By precisely measuring the kinetic energies of the resulting alphas, a new determination of the direct-decay component's fraction was achieved, yielding a value of $10.5^{+3.1}_{-2.8}$%. This result is in excellent agreement with previous findings derived from both experimental and theoretical methods.

We investigate the attractive Rashba Hubbard model featuring spin-singlet superconductivity, focusing on regimes where magnetic ordering is suppressed. By applying both mean-field theory and dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to analyze the phase diagram and superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c$), we observe that including dynamical fluctuations within a DMFT framework significantly boosts $T_c$ by orders of magnitude compared to standard mean-field estimates. Specifically, three-dimensional systems exhibit a tenfold increase, while two-dimensional systems show an eight-order-of-magnitude rise. Our findings reveal a novel phase in the phase diagram—a spin-singlet topological superconducting (TSC) phase—using tensor polynomial topology to verify its properties. Additionally, we identify a topological superconductor (TCS) phase adjacent to the ferromagnetic region, suggesting that proximity to magnetism facilitates the emergence of topological superconductivity. These results indicate that accounting for fluctuation dynamics in complex superconductors could uncover new topological superconducting states.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite, simple, and connected graph. For any two vertices $G$, define the shortest path distance between them as $\lambda_{G}(u,v)$. A set $S \subseteq V(G)$ is considered a $k$-resolving set for a given integer $k$ if every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$ satisfies $\lambda_{G}^{k}(u, v) \neq k$ such that there exists at least one $s \in S$ where the $k$-th bit of the shortest path length between $u$ and $v$ in $G$ is distinct for each chosen vertex. A set satisfying this condition is called a minimum $k$-resolving set. The metric dimension of $G$, represented by $\delta(G)$, is then the cardinality of the smallest possible $k$-resolving set.

This paper addresses several open inquiries regarding graphs with specific values for truncated metric dimension. Additionally, it establishes a metric characterization applicable to outerplanar graphs and presents new findings concerning cyclic graphs.

Neuromorphic computing offers a compelling alternative to conventional processing models for demanding applications like pattern recognition, yet the high computational requirements of their software simulation mandate efficient virtual plant architectures. These virtual platforms allow for the early-stage assessment of applications alongside embedded hardware, facilitating the identification and refinement of architectural specifications. At this foundational stage, hardware descriptions remain abstract, making simulation speed a critical factor for architectural exploration. Addressing this, we introduce a scalable SystemC Virtual Platform for neuromorphic designs, capable of accelerating simulation by leveraging all available cores through parallel execution. This system integrates an abstracted multi-core architecture with specific models of the Loihi neuromorphic chip, including its neurons, rules, and communication mechanisms. Evaluating this platform across various workloads demonstrates a significant reduction in simulation time, thereby enhancing the feasibility of studyingNW processing capabilities.

The deployment of Machine Learning in practice frequently involves placing predicted outputs within a context of uncertainty. Addressing this, we introduce **Indecision Trees**, a method for generating classification decisions for data points that fall outside a model's predicted confidence threshold. This approach extends the standard induction tree algorithm by adding a mechanism to handle cases where confidence falls below a specific limit. We evaluate Indecision Trees across two primary areas. First, we offer a theoretical analysis showing the model's ability to approximate step functions and its ability to uniformly generalize based on the amount of training data and the selected confidence threshold. Second, we demonstrate the model's practical application in constructing a systematic reasoning engine capable of navigating knowledge graphs under scenarios involving partial or incomplete information.

Time series analysis frequently employs Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) for tasks such as distance calculation and similarity searching. However, the computational cost of running DTW on every candidate in a database is a significant bottleneck for similarity searching. This study introduces PrunedDTW, a method designed to rapidly approximate nearest neighbors by abandoning the calculation of distances for unrelated data. Furthermore, we present a new technique called Early Abandoning PrunedDTZ (EA-PrunedDTW) that achieves an additional speedup. While EA-PrunedDTZ continues the warping process between two specific sequences for shorter durations compared to the previous method, EA-PrunedDTZ offers a substantial performance gain. Our experimental evaluation confirms that EA-PrunedDTZ delivers even greater efficiency than Early Abandoning PrunedDTZ.

Testing education research indicates that detailed feedback, which offers specific line-by-line corrections on bugs, is less effective than inquiry-based feedback for fostering students' testing skills. However, there is a lack of empirical data comparing how these two feedback approaches influence the specific acquisition of test design abilities. This study addresses that gap by evaluating both the impact and specific effectiveness of detailed versus inquiry-based feedback on university students' test design capabilities. Through a controlled randomized trial involving 100 participants across two groups, alongside a supplementary semi-structured interview study with 15 students, the study quantifies design skill improvements and qualitatively explores students' perspectives on these feedback mechanisms. The findings suggest that both feedback types significantly enhance test design abilities, yet inquiry-based feedback is more effective at reducing the number of critical errors. Furthermore, the qualitative insights underscore the superiority of inquiry-based feedback in engaging students, stimulating critical thinking, and fostering autonomy, while also advocating for additional qualitative research into teaching practices surrounding testing feedback.

Explainable AI (X解释able) aims to generate human-understandable accounts of how black-box models function. While prior research has developed various methods to create understandable global feature importance metrics, it is less clear how to simultaneously explain individual predictions and the model's overall logic using features and features' relationships. This paper presents a novel approach to generating such explanations for Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) by combining formal concept analysis with integer linear programming. Our method determines which concepts—formed by grouping attributes and determining their relationships—most influence a DNN's output, using an optimization process to select only the most relevant attributes for those explanations. This allows us to control the level of granularity in the created explanations. Furthermore, the approach handles both qualitative and quantitative attributes, accommodating binary, integer, and real-valued data.

Over-smoothing represents a critical challenge in graph learning, often undermining deep Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) by degrading their performance. This study provides a theoretical analysis outlining the conditions under which over-smoothing emerges and offers insights into its effects on metric convergence and node classification accuracy within the GCN framework. We first demonstrate that an over-smoothed state inevitably results as graph structures progressively blend node features across topological neighborhoods within these networks. Subsequently, through comprehensive experiments utilizing synthetic data, we validated our findings, confirming the practical impact of over-smoothing on both classification accuracy and overall model performance in real-world scenarios.

This study details a search for dark matter involving Z boson associated production at the CMS experiment during the 2018 data-taking period at CMS, operating at 13 TeV. Analysis focused on events featuring one or two charged leptons (e, μ), substantial missing transverse momentum, and significant jet activity. Several novel or enhanced control regions for background estimation were implemented, including a newly introduced tag-and-probe method to refine the single-lepton, off-shell Z signal. While no evidence for dark matter was found, these observations set the most stringent exclusion limits to date on several WIMP models, including the higgsino, mixed gaugino, and simplified model scenarios.

This paper establishes that every topological group can be represented as a long colimit involving pre-existing groups with socks. Remote epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, and lattice-mismatched (van der Waals) epitaxy represent the three primary growth modes for thin films on lattice-incommensurate substrates, yet recent advances in remote growth of magnetoelectronic multilayers on lattice-incommensurate substrates have demonstrated characteristics of pinhole epitaxial growth. This study utilizes remote epitaxial growth of the magnetoresistive material Cu₂MnAs on lithium niobate to investigate the conditions governing the transition between these epitaxial regimes. By examining the remote epitaxial growth of Cu₂MnAs on lithium niobate, this study reveals that while the film initially exhibits a remote epitaxial relationship with lithium niobate, increasing deposition temperature triggers a shift toward a pinhole epitaxial regime. This study demonstrates that this transition can be effectively suppressed by employing magnetically doped magnesium zirconate, a process that maintains the film's orientation while enhancing its crystallinity. This research provides valuable insights into epitaxial growth mechanisms, which are essential for engineering high-quality magnetoresistive devices that rely on lattice-incommensurate substrates.

This paper investigates inference regarding the common trends in a group of heavy-tailed time series that undergo structural shifts. We introduce a new class of heavy-tailed processes extending previous work by Asai and Giacomin (2017), enabling temporal evolution of both the structural break date and the break magnitude. Our proposed framework builds on the tail index estimator from Angelini, Clavié, and Klüppelberg (2019), adapted here to handle non-stationarity. Furthermore, we establish the convergence properties of a new data-driven thresholding estimator for the tail $\alpha$-mean, which represents our primary interest. Numerical simulations validate the inference procedures, and the methodology is applied to a dataset tracking global financial markets across 44 countries to assess cross-national heavy-tail characteristics and their stability over time.
