Topological T-duality represents the spectral counterpart of T-duality within superstring theory. In this study, we investigate topological twining in the context of torus bundles arising from spaces involving twisted torus structures. By explicitly demonstrating that topological twining in the case of twisted torus structures is achievable if the structure is simultaneously that of a twisted co-torus, we provide sufficient proof. We accomplish this by generalizing the spectral twining formula for topological twining, initially proposed by the current authors, to encompass these specific types of torus bundles.

Imitation learning is a widely used strategy in reinforcement learning that extracts policies from expert behavior, reducing the extensive training efforts usually required by standard reinforcement learning methods. However, most current approaches depend heavily on detailed expert action sequences, which are often difficult to acquire in real-world settings. To address this limitation, we introduce a framework capable of learning a common task from multiple imperfect expert demonstrations, where some agents provide only partial subsequences of the required actions. By modeling each expert's behavior as an implicit hidden Markov model and applying self-supervised learning to predict missing actions, our method successfully extracts a robust joint task policy. We validate this approach on several standard benchmarks, including human evaluations for the two-arm stacking task, demonstrating superior performance compared to baseline methods.

This study addresses a methodology for constructing and evaluating low-complexity asymptotically good asymptotic codes based on algebraic geometry (AAG) and periodic autocorrelation functions (PAC). We introduce an algorithm that not only achieves a theoretical distortion factor $\lambda = 1$, but also demonstrates significantly reduced computational costs compared to existing approaches. Additionally, we introduce novel asymptotic codes generated by applying our proposed algorithm to the Hamming and Jacobsthal sequences, as well as several new sequences.

We introduce a novel system designed to track hand movements and reconstitute hand-object interactions using sequential point cloud data. This sequence is generated in real time by an external, untethered RGBD sensor operating in natural environments, capturing depth for multiple hands and objects simultaneously. To achieve this, we develop an end-to-end end-to-end tracker that identifies both hands and objects, maintaining data association across frames without relying on an explicit optical flow mechanism. Once objects are localized, we reconstruct the precise geometry of the interaction by integrating the segmented color information with the corresponding point cloud segments. Extensive evaluations on both synthetic sequences and real-world captures demonstrate that our system significantly exceeds current state-of-the-art performance regarding the fidelity of the reconstructed interactions. Source code is available at https://github.com/yourname/yourrepo

This study investigates rank 4 tail-triangle C-groups characterized by an interlacing number of two. We fully determine these groups corresponding to four distinct Coxeter diagrams and position them relative to existing classification efforts while addressing a specific open query in this domain.

This paper introduces a novel framework for learning markerless calibration and end-effort pose estimation utilizing depth cameras, diverging from conventional methods by eschewing explicit geometric constraints such as known corner features or camera intraparameters. Instead, the approach leverages a large dataset of image-depth pairs to automatically detect local feature descriptors and learn an implicit geometric calibration model as well as a pose estimation function. Experiments utilizing both simulated and real-world datasets validate the model's geometric accuracy and learned calibration precision, with results comparable to those achieved by methods relying on known geometric intraparameters. Furthermore, the system achieves competitive performance on the YCB Visual Pose Estimation benchmark.

We introduce a treatment interference framework wherein a unit's response relies exclusively on its treatment condition and the treatment status of other units within its K-neighborhood. While existing methods for identifying interference rely on tailored randomized experiments and conditioning-based tests that assume non-interference among treated neighbors for non-interceded units, our approach diverges by explicitly targeting those specifically designed for interference detection. Our methodology leverages a randomized experiment establishing units into either the treatment or control groups and examines the conditionality of the overall response variable on treatment group membership and the specific conditionality on the group's size in those not receiving treatment but whose neighbors do. We propose two distinct tests: one utilizing treatment group labels and another employing group size data. Our results indicate that incorporating group information into these tests enhances power compared to traditional approaches. We further provide sufficient conditions for the consistency of our test statistics and demonstrate through simulations that our procedures outperform existing methods in terms of power.

We investigate neutrino production mechanisms resulting from self-annihilation of dark matter particles within the early thermal environment of neutron stars. Our findings indicate that these radiative processes can substantially elevate specific neutrino luminosities—by factors reaching up to $10^{13}$ in certain scenarios—compared to standard thermal production. These dramatic increases could potentially dominate the total neutrino output of neutron stars, thereby enabling more stringent constraints on both the neutrino mass matrix and dark matter parameters.

Driven by machine learning advancements, there is a growing trend toward replacing conventional physics-based simulations with data-based models due to their superior computational efficiency. These data-driven models, trained on historical data, aim to replicate the core behaviors of their physics-based counterparts. A primary challenge remains the heavy data requirements for these new models, a problem that becomes acute when historical data is scarce—a situation frequently encountered in scientific research and engineering. To address this, this paper introduces a novel "cooperative data-driven modeling" approach. By training multiple models cooperatively on limited historical data to mimic a physics-based model, it enables knowledge sharing that reduces data needs. The framework further includes a feedback loop where each individual model receives performance data based on how well the collective group replicates the target. This creates incentives for each model to improve, fostering competition that collectively enhances accuracy. We validate the approach using two case studies: approximating a computationally expensive homogenization technique for composite materials and a reduced-order model for the Navier-Stokes equations. The results confirm that cooperative data-driven models achieve accuracy comparable to that of physics-based methods while requiring significantly less training data.

Recent research into large-scale language models (LLMs) has revealed their remarkable capacity for in-context learning. Nevertheless, little is known about how different pretraining corpora affect this ability. In this paper, we investigate this aspect by examining three distinct pretraining strategies: (1) using only WebText, (2) using only Wikipedia, and (3) using a diverse collection of internet texts. Our findings demonstrate that pretraining data variety significantly alters the model's learning performance. Specifically, we observe that a model trained on web documents excels at mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, whereas a model trained on encyclopedic texts like Wikipedia shows superior performance in factual query answering. Furthermore, we analyze how these corpus variations impact reasoning across multiple steps versus single steps. Our results indicate that blending pretraining datasets enhances overall efficiency in generating responses, while web-based data continues to drive superior performance in specialized domains such as mathematics and programming.

We investigate the formation and evolution of cold clouds within galaxy clusters using radiative-hydrodynamic simulations. Crucially, the long-term stability of these clouds relies on their initial conditions; they remain stable for extended durations if they begin with high internal turbulence and low magnetic field strengths. We further demonstrate that cloud fragmentation is intrinsically linked to the internal magnetic field strength, as well as thermal conduction, which collectively dictate the resulting cloud mass and size.

Consequently, when expressed in terms of four-velocity or light-cone coordinates, the necessary energy density follows a non-uniform (anisotropic) spatial profile. Furthermore, by integrating this velocity-dependent energy density over a spatial weight function to compute a transverse momentum spectrum, we obtain $dN/dp_T dp_T dy$ distributions that align qualitatively with experimental observations, exhibiting a peak at a non-zero $p_T$ rather than solely at zero.

While high-velocity protostellar jets are well-documented, low-velocity outflows remain less understood. Since both phenomena are driven by the collimated ejection of material from forming stars, a potential causal relationship exists. This study investigates the influence of jets on outflows using the hydrodynamical code RAMSES, simulating the accretion process of a 0.3 solar mass star with an inclined magnetic torus. The model reveals that the ejection of mass from the disk torus generates a broad, collimated low-velocity stream perpendicular to the star, consistent with protostellar jets. Additionally, the focused radiation from this radiation torus enhances the photoevaporative efficiency of the outflow. Although jets do not solely account for the full extent of outflows, the results indicate that they can significantly influence outflow characteristics and may offer valuable insights into the early stages of outflow development.

This study tackles the problem of achieving equilibrium between performance and saturation limits in a specific class of constrained nonlinear systems. By utilizing non-linear barrier functions, the authors propose a balanced control framework. This approach guarantees that the closed-loop system remains asymptotically stable while ensuring that tracking errors stay strictly within predefined bounds. Furthermore, the proposed control strategy ensures that saturation limits are not exceeded, while pushing system performance as close to these limits as feasible.

This study presents analytical estimates for the short-term (biennial) resonances affecting Earth's orbit caused by solar radiation pressure, building on previous work by Liou (2006). It then extends this approach to generate generalized estimates for all resonant cases involving Earth, Mars, and the Sun that may arise from radiation pressure. These new formulas are valid with respect to the orbital elements of the test particle and cover a broad spectrum of scenarios across the solar system. Finally, the paper compares these estimates with numerical calculations of the exact resonance curves; such comparisons demonstrate that the method yields highly accurate results, particularly for short-term resonances.

We introduce an efficient method for creating Hamiltonians that describe light-matter interactions in the presence of optical fields, based on first-principles electronic structure theory. By incorporating the vector potential into the input files for density functional theory (specifically using the tight-binding approach), we generate corresponding many-body Hamiltonians. This framework has been implemented within the $\text{CP2K}$ software package. We demonstrate the approach using photodetection in graphene as a石墨烯 example, showing how to derive selection rules and light absorption characteristics. Furthermore, we validate the model's universal applicability by studying radiative recombination in silicon quantum dots.

Object pose estimation is fundamental to robotics and computer vision, yet estimating the 6 degrees of freedom (6-DoF) pose of a single instance from a single image remains difficult due to infinite ambiguities regarding size, shape, and pose. This paper introduces a categor-level object pose estimation framework that assumes access to a library of semantic keypoints for the object category in question. We propose two methods: 1) a robust 2D-based approach that estimates pose by optimizing a category-level semantic constraint derived from a pre-learned 3D shape model; and 2) a robust3D approach that simultaneously refines both individual and category-level 3D shapes while estimating object pose by optimizing a dual-object optimization objective. We further develop an iterative algorithm capable of estimating 6-DoF poses from 3D point clouds while updating 3D shape parameters. Comprehensive experiments on synthetic data and the NYU-V2 real-world dataset confirm that our proposed frameworks significantly surpass existing state-of-the-art methodologies.

We introduce an innovative confidence interval method tailored for distributions with confidence levels adjustable at will, exemplified here by using a Cauchy distribution. This approach constructs intervals directly from the sample dataset without relying on asymptotic theory or assuming a specific underlying form, a feature that becomes possible due to the unique properties of order statistics within a uniform distribution. By applying inversion to the cumulative distribution function, high-confidence intervals are generated for various distributions, such as the standard normal and the Cauchy. While intervals for a Cauchy distribution derived via the empirical mean have previously been published, our novel methodology successfully extends this to estimators based on both the empirical median and the combined median–mean.

Basket trials are increasingly recognized as a viable clinical research format for evaluating multiple subgroups simultaneously. By allowing treatment effects to be shared across these groups, basket trials can reduce sample sizes without compromising statistical power. This study introduces a methodology for calculating sample requirements for basket trials that incorporate historical data. Our approach utilizes a multivariate model to analyze current and historical treatment responses, assuming a multivariate normal distribution for observed outcomes. By applying Bayesian inference, we establish a hierarchical structure to borrow information among distinct subpopulations. Relying on a Bayesian framework, our proposed method determines sample sizes by identifying numbers sufficient to achieve precisions meeting predetermined standards. This numerical technique is validated through simulations based on various multivariate scenarios. Applied to data from a NCI-sponsored basket trial targeting various cancers with BRAF V600E mutations, we demonstrate the procedure's utility in determining appropriate sample sizes for concurrent open-label treatments.

The industry demand for extremely accurate movements is driving significant progress in high-precision technology. Among various control strategies, the Sequential Loop Closing (SLC) approach stands out for its ability to enhance loop performance by dynamically adjusting bandwidths based on the specific command type. However, a critical limitation arises when mechanical systems operate under large position variations, as the fixed plant model used in standard SLC applications becomes inaccurate. This flaw causes the designated bandwidths to deviate from their target values, preventing optimal controller configuration. To resolve such discrepancies, this study proposes applying SLC in combination with a flexible, data-driven Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) model. By employing the Flexible Data-Driven (FDD) technique, which eliminates reliance on system identification, these precise LPV models can be constructed directly from experimental data. This research demonstrates both the concept and feasibility of high-precision motion control through a hardware implementation that couples SRC with high-fidelity, data-driven LPV models.

We introduce PRNet, a universal deep learning framework for rigid partial-to-partial registration, capable of aligning inputs whether they are partial volumes, pairs of partial volumes, or full volumes. This model is trained using self-supervised learning, relying on the alignment loss between predicted deformations and ground truth mappings derived from methods like PRNet. Notably, the entire training process is conducted without requiring paired data or explicit ground truth physical properties. This deep learning approach demonstrates significant potential in enhancing the speed and precision of medical image alignment. Additionally, PRNets exhibits remarkable generative power, successfully regenerating high-quality structures for missing data surrounding the input field.

A group $G$ exhibits the property $R_\infty$ precisely when the count of orbits under conjugation on its first cohomology (relative to the group, denoted $H^1(G,G)$) associated with an automorphism is infinite, implying that for any derivation $d$ of $G$, the number of conjugated orbits of $\operatorname{der}(G)$ is infinite. This study introduces the concept of a nilpotent class $c$ Baumslag-Solair group as any class that defines a nilpotent quotient of a group, and we demonstrate that their derived subgroup always exhibits the $R_\infty$ property. Additionally, we introduce and investigate the property $\tilde{R}_\infty$ within the framework of extensions of groups. It is shown that for a short exact homomorphism sequence $1\to N\to E\to Q\to 1$, if $N$ exhibits $\tilde{R}_\infty$ property and $N$'s normal in $E$, then $E$ inherits this property too. Furthermore, findings indicate a general condition ensuring the property $\tilde{R}_\infty$ for groups, and theory reveals the property $\tilde{R}_\infty$ for generalized solvable nilpotent class.

Recent SM vacuum stability analyses indicate that even within the minimal extension involving a single scalar, significant room exists for this phenomenon. We introduce the "collider landscape" concept, examining how various experimental facilities could map parameter spaces allowing for either a metastable or completely stable vacuum. Using reach probability density functions to assess potential discoveries, our analysis suggests that an $e^+e^-$ collider is best positioned to delineate vacuum stability boundaries in low-to-intermediate mass regions ($m < 100$ GeV), while a hadron collider excels for higher mass scenarios ($m > 100$ GeV).

We introduce a trajectory-basis, forward-optimization-based approach for inversion time-resolved ultrafast experiments, demonstrating its application across three scenarios: a one-dimensional model for time-resolved gain spectroscopy, a two-dimensional model for pump-probe spectroscopy, and a two-dimensional simulated X-ray scattering study for a peptide. Beyond describing these applications, we provide the theoretical justification for generalizing this method from one to higher dimensions and include a comparison with conventional maximum-likelihood estimation.

This study calculates meson light-front wave functions and distribution amplitudes for $D$ and $D_s$ families using the light-front Bethe-Salpeter formalism, specifically targeting $C$ and $C'$ states. We employ a relativistic constituent quark model to solve for the Bethe-Salpeter wave functions by addressing the equal-time projection and meson mass constraints. Our results for derived distribution amplitudes are contrasted with prior literature findings.

This research establishes the equivalence between various Gelfand-Philo spaces of type $\mathcal{F}sh_{1,s}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and specific classes of Fourier transforms, simultaneously verifying their non-trivial nature. Additionally, we explore applications concerning those Toeplitz operators on the Fock space for which their symbols belong to $\mathcal{Fsh_{1,s}(\mathbb{R}^n)}$.

Segmenting instances in unlabeled medical imaging remains a major hurdle for deep learning, largely due to the scarcity of annotated data and domain shifts caused by variations in imaging settings and institutions. While self-supervised learning has been explored to address this, it often demands extensive computational resources and complex training pipelines. This paper introduces a streamlined approach that requires no additional preprocessing or architectural modifications, leveraging the segmentation generator within existing frameworks. Specifically, we frame the problem as a cyclic segmentation setup and employ a segmentation generative adversarial network to align across different data domains. Experiments conducted on two prominent datasets—Pancreas and Prostate—demonstrate that our method enhances segmentation accuracy and generalization. Compared to leading supervised techniques, our approach yields competitive performance while maintaining simplicity.

This study introduces a new scheme for representing and predicting human actions using feature mappings within recurrent neural networks (RNNs). A key component is the use of kernelized feature maps to represent both static and dynamic action features. These representations are generated by applying kernel expansion principles to kernel perceptron and kernelized local dimensionality reduction techniques, alongside the development of two new feature maps: kernelized support plane indicator and kernelized support line indicator. Experimental evaluations across the NTURGB+D-129, UTD-MotionBank, and Microsoft Kinetics datasets demonstrate superior or competitive performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study utilizes the model of NUV photospheric and chromospheric radiation developed by Hu et al. (2009) to simulate the observed NUV flare intensities. By establishing that first-order deformations of such instantons correspond precisely to certain pure imaginary anti-self-dual instanton forms, the authors demonstrate that these deformations map into specific moduli spaces of these forms. Furthermore, a connection is detailed connecting these instanton moduli spaces with the moduli space of the underlying nearly parallel G₂ structure.

Point cloud models have emerged as a significant advancement in deep learning for 3D scene understanding. Similar to ImageNet, which facilitates performance gains in computer vision through large-scale modeling, extensive datasets are necessary to train robust point cloud models. However, due to limited point cloud annotation efforts, these datasets remain small, hindering a point cloud model's ability to generalize on complex scenarios. This paper introduces Transform-Specific Smoothing (TPC), a data smoothing technique that enhances model capacity without requiring additional data. TPC functions by adding stochastic transformations to input point clouds, which are subsequently used to train the model. Transformations are randomly selected from a predefined set, and training remains consistent with standard data augmentation practices. Transformations are also applied to the output point clouds, and the trained model is evaluated across various 3D scene types. Transformations are chosen based on their ability to improve training data without increasing model complexity, and they are designed to learn specific transformation invariants. This approach enhances the model's ability to generalize across diverse 3D environments.

This study investigates the network performance of slot-structured ALOHA and CSMA protocols in FMCW radar systems. The objective is to evaluate how network design parameters and traffic loads affect collision probability and throughput. The work begins by detailing the standard Operation Modes for FMCW radars and then restructures both the slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols into traffic-simulation-compatible formats. Subsequently, both protocols are modeled using Markov chains to derive closed-form expressions for key performance metrics, specifically collision probability and throughput. The paper further establishes a relationship between these metrics and well-known queuing models, enabling comparison with alternative networking protocols for FMCW radar applications.

This study presents theoretical findings on how spectral resolution influences the observation of Entangled Two-Photon Absorption (ETPA) using Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference experiments. We develop a formalism to calculate the coincidence counts retrieved at two detectors, taking into account the spectral characteristics of both the absorbing material and the HOM setup. Furthermore, we analytically demonstrate that enhancing the spectral resolution of the readout amplifies the visible ETPA signal. These predictions are supported by analytical proofs and additional simulations.

We determine the $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology of $\mathbf{C}P(V)$ for a complex vector space $V$ under the standard linear group action. The findings demonstrate a correspondence with cohomology of a specific abelian variety that depends on the representation $V$.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) aims to predict missing information in knowledge graphs by incorporating temporal signals, a task that has attracted significant interest due to broad applications in various domains. This study introduces a simple yet highly effective approach for temporal knowledge graph reasoning, relying on a model-independent, sparse low-rank representation of temporal evidence. By leveraging the specific structure of the evidence, this proposed method enhances both the accuracy and the generalizability of existing temporal graph embedding models. Furthermore, we introduce a novel representation learning framework designed with theoretical guarantees to achieve a model-specific optimal balance between precision and recall. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in the leading dynamic embedding techniques.

While research on the acoustic benefits of the piano's soundboard is extensive, the influence of ground sound traveling through the soundbridge remains understudied. This study utilizes audio recorded with two microphones positioned above an piano to isolate the impact of ground sound. By playing a calibrated impulse and analyzing the data with a known hammer impact reference, a second microphone placed above the string captures the hammer sound alongside structural transmission. Because these pathways differ significantly in duration, the contribution of ground sound can be determined. Our findings reveal that even from a high perspective, ground sound is audible and enhances acoustic projection, particularly for lower frequencies.

This research presents an unambiguous proof of Bell nonlocality, free from the limitations of the standard Bell inequality approach, derived from correlations that are not perfectly correlated. We demonstrate that while previously unreported in quantum optics literature, these correlations arise naturally in systems involving single photons passing through beam splitters. Consequently, this methodology offers a robust framework for establishing local realism violation in experiments where coincidence counts are subject to noise or background interference, complementing the widely used Bell inequality strategy.

Hydrogen-rich materials are frequently proposed as candidates for high-temperature superconductivity due to their exceptional chemical stability, high compressibility, and robust metallic character. In this study, we investigate hydrogen boride (H12B), a recently synthesized compound, using first-principles calculations. Our findings indicate that H12B possesses a bulk modulus of 182 GPa and a high density of states at the Fermi level, suggesting strong superconducting potential. We further estimate a critical superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) between 100 K and 200 K for this material at ambient pressure. Notably, this predicted $T_c$ is significantly higher than previously reported values for hydrogen monoboride ($C_3H_3B$) and hydrogen-trifborite ($C_3H_3B$) compounds.

This paper investigates runs of identical elements in uniformly distributed integer partitions modeled as Young-Feynman diagrams drawn in the first quadrant. By applying Fibonacci-based scaling to these parts, the text analyzes the limiting behavior of run lengths as the partition's total sum $n$ increases toward infinity. Specifically, it determines the limiting probability distribution for each individual run and establishes joint distributions across the set of all runs. These findings are then utilized to compute key statistical measures—including means, central moments, and coefficients of variation and skewness—demonstrating that their dependence on $n$ follows a quadratic polynomial pattern, with specific formulas derived for the first two coefficients of variation.

This study investigates amenability within arithmetic groups, deriving new results by charmenability and stiffness. We construct infinite families of STF groups characterized by an amenability at the top level, alongside presenting several new examples of stiff groups, including newly discovered infinite families.

This paper presents the formal specification and verification of a fail-operational driving system. Initially, the dual objectives of the system are defined: to maintain safe travel during safety-critical failures of the actuation layer while also enabling travel continuity. Following this, the architectural framework is developed to support these aims, emphasizing its capacity for straightforward verification under complex verification goals. Subsequently, the multistate safety state machine and the multi-input multi-output (MIMO) safety system are formulated within a fail-operational architecture to uphold system safety across all operational states. Furthermore, the dual redundancy safety mechanism and the fail-operational safety manager are verified individually within their specific contexts. Concluding the work, both the myopic and non-myopic approaches for maintaining safe travel are formally verified within the designated system architecture.

This study introduces a novel, data-driven clustering approach for dynamical systems that relies solely on time series to capture both external and internal system dynamics. By constructing a novel influence operator, we define a measurement of mutual informationR based exclusively on available time series data. This enables the creation of a clustering framework that partitions the system into distinct groups by maximizing inter-clusterR and minimizing intra-clusterR. The proposed method's data-driven nature makes it particularly suitable for use with black-box systems where the full analytical form ofR is unknown or inaccessible. We validate this framework through experiments on simplified models of gene regulatory networks and through an analysis of transcriptome data from the human embryonic cerebral cortex, demonstrating its efficacy in complex, data-rich environments.

This paper examines how three prominent approaches to differentiating between Leibniz's infinitesimals and their modern viability as foundations for his calculus. It focuses on the challenges posed by the conflicts among those procedures and the difficulties they create for establishing his methods.

Using the $k$-space perturbation theory approach, we calculate neutral hydrogen intensity fluctuations as observed by interferometers to the fourth order. By applying an expansion in conformal time and leveraging the primordial power spectrum, the spectral index, and the linear matter power spectrum, the required higher-order correlation functions are determined. To enhance computational efficiency, convolution operations within these correlations are optimized through a "convolution reduction" technique. Subsequently, we derive the halo model predictions for these correlations and quantify the signal contribution from different halos based on their virial temperatures. Additionally, we assess the impact of foreground removal, demonstrating that even with aggressive cuts eliminating power at low $k$, neutral hydrogen intensity mappings remain viable. This contamination affects only approximately 10% of the total neutral hydrogen signal, resulting in negligible errors for dark energy studies. Finally, we estimate the achievable dark energy precision using a fiducial LSS model and an optimistic instrument configuration, concluding that neutral hydrogen intensity mapping could achieve $\Delta w_0 \sim 0.01$ and $\Delta w_0a \sim 0.1$ by the year 2025.

This paper introduces a user-centric hybrid recommender system designed to address the limitations inherent in both document-based and user-based collaborative filtering approaches. By incorporating documents derived from user profiles to enhance context-collaborative fusion, and simultaneously leveraging a document-based component to mitigate sparsity and cold-start issues, our method offers significant improvements. We conducted an empirical evaluation of our system using three real-world datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms several state-of-the-art baseline algorithms.

In this study, we establish the conditions under which free randomness of $B$ arises within $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and provide a characterization of when two unitarily invariant random matrices are freely independent of $$-type $A$ and $B$, respectively. Our results rely on a distinctive approach centered on conditional freeness with respect to $M_n(\mathbb C)^{op}$. Additionally, the concept of infimal independence of $$$-type $A$ and $B$ is defined and discussed.

This study revisits the monitoring of real-time properties expressed in Timed Automata (TAs) and extends the framework to handle networks of timed properties (Ntas). While our initial approach for single TAs achieved a worst-case state complexity matching the minimal supertautomaton constructed for a given property, this paper generalizes the algorithm to network cases. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm based on the product of a property network and system state system, demonstrating that the resulting complexity is significantly lower in terms of system states compared to the supertautomaton method. Furthermore, we propose a variant utilizing the theory of convex corners for time constraints, which shifts complexity to the property model instead of the system. In this new strategy, the worst-case state complexity is halved relative to the traditional supertautomata technique.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera, known as ACQ, is engineered to obtain and fine-tune the pointing alignment and optical inputs for the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLT) instrument GRAVITY. As an actively focused, three-telescope shearing interferometer, its design enables the direct measurement of wavefront coherence across the combining lasers and pupil alignment of the main instruments. Operating within spectral bands from 470 to 900 nm and an angular field of 100 arcsec, it offers spatial resolution reaching approximately 0.03 arcsec. This text outlines the system's design and operational capabilities while evaluating key performance metrics, including telescope pointing stability, beam alignment quality, and the precision of wavefront sensing.

The generalized $k$-center problem involves selecting a subset of $k$ cluster centers from a given point set to ensure the largest cluster diameter is minimized. We introduce a parameterized approach for solving this problem, relying on either the path highway dimension or the Doubling Conjecture associated with the metric space. We establish a parameterized algorithm grounded in a path-hypergraph scheme, effectively limiting the search for optimal centers to a manageable subset. By leveraging this framework, we derive a new approach for resolving the metric Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP). Specifically, we define a subset of nodes from which a metric TSP tour can be constructed to achieve a $\alpha$-approximation ratio, where this subset's size is determined by either the path highway dimension or the metric dimension derived from the conjectured doubling property. This methodology yields a first algorithm capable of nearly linearly processing instances of metric TSP with bounded highway dimension. Furthermore, we formulate a variation of the problem termed "bounded-diameter TSP," which requires finding a subset of size proportional to the input size such that all nodes can be linked via a $\alpha$-approximate metric TSP. This concept establishes a clear distinction between path highway dimension and standard dimension in the context of these optimization problems.

This paper focuses on solving polynomial linear systems with coefficient evaluation at random nodes, focusing on both theoretical bounds and practical performance. We establish new complexity upper bounds for identifying all real roots, potentially stopping early if enough information is gathered. Consequently, we derive identical sharp limits for deciding system satisfiability. A key feature of these results is their independence from the number of parameters, contrasting with previous methods. Furthermore, we introduce a sophisticated algorithm capable of reducing system degree via coordinate changes, thereby decreasing the required random evaluations for root-fascination.

This study investigates the symmetry-emitted particle pairs parity maintained by chiral topological materials, specifically focusing on two-dimensional fermionic systems with $ \text{V}_\text{T} = 1 $. We identify a class of paritiesymmetrical-bounded states (PBES) characterized by balanced counts of left and right moving modes on each boundary. These states exhibit stability against perturbations that respect the parity symmetry, allowing for the controlled release of duality-bounded fermionic excitations. Our findings reveal that topological invariants can be expressed as linear combinations of various contributions from left moving modes, thereby establishing a direct link between the internal structure of paritiesymmetrical-bounded states and observable quantities in experiment. Finally, we outline potential strategies to engineer such systems using realistic setups within actual experiments.

We introduce a straightforward yet precise analytical model describing the equilibrium thermodynamics of alkali metals, which feature a non-trivial, bound-state-inclusive electronic structure. This structural complexity significantly impacts the chemical potential and excites states that traditional plasma models, reliant on simplified assumptions about neutral atoms, often overlook. By explicitly accounting for these bound-state characteristics, our derived chemical potential formula addresses the deficiencies found in conventional alkali plasma theories. Consequently, this new expression enhances the predictability accuracy for alkali-related plasma properties, including ionization fraction, chemical potential, and screening length.

This study explores the spectral properties of vector mesons within a hot medium exhibiting both temperature temperatures and fermionic chiral asymmetry. We apply the Keldysh formalism alongside finite temperature quantum field theory to derive the spectral function of the $\rho$-meson, utilizing a chiral Lagrangian framework where the chiral symmetry breaking sector interacts with a background of medium-generated fermions showing chiral asymmetry. Our analysis reveals that this asymmetry influences $\rho$-meson spectral properties primarily through the mass term of the mesons' longitudinal component, driven by its coupling with the pseudoscalar component of $\rho$-mesons. We further employ a hidden local symmetry approach to calculate the same spectral function, finding that while the results exhibit a more pronounced dependence on chiral asymmetry than the previous method suggested, they ultimately yield physically consistent conclusions.

We investigate the fundamental task of estimating a network's node count alongside its degree distribution, operating in a setting where a subset of nodes is Byzantine and can send arbitrary messages to all other nodes with some communication noise. Assuming the network possesses a small-world structure, our approach leverages the popular "time-to-live" (ttl) method. We establish that for small-world networks, the standard deviation of the ttl-based estimator is significantly lower compared to random graphs of the same size, resulting in superior performance even when compromised by Byzantine agents. Furthermore, our analysis provides a network size estimate achievable by all non-compromised nodes with high confidence. This bound scales nearly linearly with the count of non-compromised nodes and depends logarithmically on both the total network size and the proportion of total nodes that are Byzantine.

Long short-term series prediction is a highly demanded yet difficult challenge in many fields. Although existing methods based on recurrent neural networks and deep learning show some potential for learning from historical dependencies, they often fail to generalize well to future predictions. Recently, deep graph convolutional networks have emerged as a powerful tool for mapping multi-dimensional time series data to a graph structure, effectively capturing the underlying dynamics. This paper introduces AGCN, a new framework that automatically constructs graphs for multidimensional time series prediction, overcoming the limitations of current methods that require pre-defined graph topologies. By using a multi-fidelity search algorithm to optimize an objective function based on prediction accuracy, AGCN automatically determines the optimal graph structure. Furthermore, the framework employs a multi-output prediction mechanism to forecast all future time steps simultaneously, rather than iteratively predicting one step at a time. Experimental results on various multidimensional time series show that AGCN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Atmospheric dispersion (atmospheric chromatic refraction) is a phenomenon where light rays from celestial objects bend differently depending on their wavelength as they enter Earth's atmosphere. This effect is a significant source of error in high-precision astronomical measurements, particularly for instruments operating in the visible and near-UV spectra, as it primarily manifests as an apparent shift in position toward the source's location in the sky. Because of its wavelength-dependent nature, atmospheric dispersion can be approximated using linear equations in visible and near-UV bands, with coefficients that vary based on the observer's location, the source's altitude, and the specific model employed. This study focuses on determining the characteristics of atmospheric dispersion models using real observational data collected by the 1.2-meter GTC telescope. Specifically, we analyze residuals generated by various models to evaluate their fit against actual measurements. Our findings indicate that linear models generally achieve a precision of about 1 milliarcsecond (mas), with an average root-mean-square residual of 0.85 mas. Given this level of accuracy, atmospheric dispersion represents a minor component of the total residual variance in our measurements, which also include contributions from the image quality limit imposed by seeing conditions.

Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous NLP tasks, yet their large model sizes and computational complexity continue to hinder widespread deployment. Knowledge distillation offers a viable solution by compressing these models into smaller, more efficient architectures. Most existing distillation methods optimize for a single aggregate target, which discards the valuable differential information contained within individual teacher outputs critical for fine-grained task resolution. Addressing this limitation, we introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel multi-teacher distillation framework that iteratively harnesses ensemble logits from multiple teachers while preserving inter-logit relationships. PILE distorts the learning process to accommodate teacher knowledge hierarchies: in even iteration steps, it employs an aggressive pairwise loss to amplify the contrast between student predictions for distinct token classes, whereas odd steps utilize standard ensemble loss to facilitate knowledge transfer. This alternating strategy facilitates rapid student exploration of the solution space alongside effective feature extraction. Experiments conducted on the distillation of GPT-2 and RoBERTa demonstrate that PILE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, delivering substantial gains in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Code for this project can be accessed at https://github.com/jianhao2017/pi le.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) can be represented by a real scalar field featuring a mass scale around $10^{-23}$ eV $\leq m \leq 10^{-11}$ eV. This field is hypothesized to form a coherent state with a slowly varying envelope modulated at a frequency $f \approx m$. This paper investigates such signatures through intensity interferometry, specifically focusing on correlated fluctuations in flux from astrophysical sources like the CMB, quasars, and the galactic center. This approach relies on measuring the second-order coherence function, $g^{(2)}(\tau)$, which exhibits a narrow peak at the UBDM frequency. Given that the spectral line's width is significantly smaller than its spacing, detecting UBDM via this method functions as an extremely precise narrowband filter. Our analysis evaluates achievable sensitivities for various detector configurations, including pairs of telescopes, radio arrays, and networks of cavities.

This study examines the continuum basis pursuit problem:
\[
\min_{f \in L^1(\mu)} \|f\|_1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad Af = g,
\]
where the operator $Af$ is defined by the integral $\int_{\Omega} k(x, \xi) \, d|\mu|( \xi)$, with $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $g \in L^1(\mu)$, $\mu$ being a given positive regular finite measure, and $k$ a given kernel. We demonstrate that a solution exists and is continuous with respect to the input data $g$ and measure $\mu$ under certain conditions, while also establishing additional conditions that guarantee uniqueness. Furthermore, we provide examples showing that these uniqueness criteria are optimal.

The P4 language has emerged as the standard for specifying programmable switch architectures, primarily focusing on match-condition based, reconfigurable table structures. Initially introduced with sample backends covering commercial hardware, P4 compiler support has historically been limited. This study presents an open-source P4 compiler backend tailored specifically to match-condition match-table architectures. Designed to run on existing reconfigurable hardware with a demonstrated area efficiency overhead of less than 10% compared to hand-optimized designs, this work expands both the range of supported target machines and the overall body of available P4 implementations.

In finite element simulations of incompressible fluid flow, a common discretisation approach involves using lowest-order Raviart-Thomas elements for the velocity field and mixed lowest-order finite elements for both the pressure and the approximated pressure gradient divergence. This study examines accurate discretisation methods for the vector transport equation ($\partial_t \mathbf{u} + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{f}$) applied to this specific setup. We demonstrate that a straightforward upwind scheme can substantially boost accuracy by roughly an order of magnitude compared to the preceding benchmark. Furthermore, we introduce a technique for estimating the resulting approximation error in the $L^2$ norm.

The significant advancements in artificial intelligence and machine learning have fueled the growth of federated collaborative systems, enabling multiple clients to jointly train a global model without sharing their sensitive local datasets. Nevertheless, real-world applications reveal inherent biases in these systems, largely stemming from the non-representative nature of client data distributions and the unequal allocation of communication resources. Simultaneously, concerns regarding data confidentiality have made differential privacy a standard requirement for securing user information. This study unites the challenges of fairness, privacy, and security within federated environments by proposing a differentially private model aggregation framework that accommodates clients with varying computational and communication capabilities. By revealing the theoretical link among fairness, privacy, and aggregation robustness against biased data contributions, we demonstrate that applying privacy-preserving techniques to the model aggregation process can mitigate information leakage from client datasets while ensuring a fair final global model. Our experimental evaluations across several canonical federated tasks validate the effectiveness of this approach.

Analysis of $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-momentum energies of 7 and 8 TeV, with $6.1\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ and $6.3\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ respectively, reports evidence for an excited $B_c^+$ state, denoted as ${\bf X}_{b\bar c}$. Recent advances in efficiently solving Hamiltonian numerics resulted in introducing a family energy-conserving Runge-Kutta techniques that generalize multi-stage methods on the run of the board stage. In this article, we generalize these R-K methods for addressing general types of differential issues and develop their continuous analog.

Model-parallel deep learning has emerged as a scalable approach for training large-scale neural networks by enabling the distributed processing of increasingly massive architectures across distributed systems. Nevertheless, conventional techniques for training these model-parallel networks rely on local critics to guide the neural optimization process. Because designing effective local critics remains a challenging and ad-hoc task, this paper proposes a unified model-parallel training algorithm that eliminates the reliance on them. By distributing both neural networks and stochastic gradient descent solvers, our method ensures that all components of the training pipeline can be trained locally without using so. This innovative approach not only automates the previously difficult design of local critics but also enhances the model-parallel training process by establishing a consistent framework.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering systems can exhibit Wada boundaries, linking basins associated with unstable periodic orbits of differing periods. This study investigates how weak dissipation influences the dynamics of such systems, specifically targeting the drive and strengthening of these Wada boundaries. Our results demonstrate that introducing Wada boundaries in 3D is inherently possible through simple and straightforward mechanisms, with only minimal and specific levels of energy loss required to generate them. Notably, the discrete nature of Wada boundaries in this context allows driven-homogeneous maps to induce them on driven-two-dimensional homogeneous maps merely by altering the system's dimensionality. Additionally, we observe that these configurations present novel pathways for driving two specific basin types that were previously inaccessible.

We propose a light boson model featuring an accidental stability mechanism that enables flavor-violating interactions. In this framework, the boson's mass is set by an electroweak-scale cutoff, while its longevity arises from violations of a global $U(1)$ symmetry broken only by exponentially suppressed effects. This approach naturally generates $|\Delta F| = 2$ transitions, offering a potential explanation for the excess observed in neutral meson mixing, specifically the $B_{s}^{0}\to \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay.

Recognizing human actions in uncurated video streams is a difficult yet essential challenge within the field of video analysis. Although current state-of-the-art methods typically depend on handcrafted features or extensive pre-trained models, these approaches often lack generalization and are inefficient. This study presents a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) designed to overcome these limitations by leveraging spatial-temporal cues to identify and track semantic action features across consecutive video frames. The method offers an alternative to prior generic recognition techniques by eliminating the dependency on manual feature engineering or pre-existing models. By incorporating this hierarchical attention mechanism, the framework effectively suppresses background noise while amplifying discriminative information, thereby enhancing the robustness of action recognition. Experimental outcomes on two prominent public datasets, TUB-BBEVP and UCF101, demonstrate that the proposed HAN achieves superior performance compared to comparable state-of-the-art methods.

The dynamics of the nonextremal Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m anti-de Sitter black/dot in the presence of a scalar field are investigated. First, a first-order differential equation describing the temporal evolution of the scalar field's mass is derived. Subsequently, the first and second laws of thermodynamics for this system are examined. It is demonstrated that the scalar field's dissipation aligns with these thermodynamic laws, thereby supporting the validity of the no-loss theorem. Furthermore, the weak cosmic censorship conjecture (WCSC) within this context is analyzed using a non-perturbative approach. The WCSC is verified in all scenarios, including cases where energy is transmitted into the black hole. Additionally, the article examines how the scalar field's influence affects the applicability of the first-order laws of the WCSC.

This piece provides a brief overview of the principles surrounding star formation and its evolution based on observational evidence, showing that it is particularly meaningful in this light as the creation of planets relies on similar processes of stellar development.

While entropy serves as a standard metric for characterizing disordered systems, its practical calculation often encounters the common "curse of degeneracy," particularly within the context of combinatorial optimization where system states correspond to partitioning levels. This work demonstrates that the Nested Sampling (NS) algorithm not only calculates entropy but also addresses two additional challenges: the dominant states problem in combinatorial optimization and the dominant states problem in statistical mechanics. We illustrate these capabilities using the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model for statistical mechanics and the Traveling Salesman Problem for optimization.

Network attacks on embedded devices are becoming increasingly common, necessitating solutions that are both effective and efficient for devices with restricted resources. This paper introduces NB coded, a lightweight attack classification framework designed to minimize memory and processing overhead while maintaining high classification accuracy. At its core, NB coded leverages a Naive Bayes classifier applied to frequency- and time-based features derived from system logs. To reduce data dimensionality and speed up classification, it employs two specific techniques: (1) sorting log entries by frequency to retain only the top 10 most common log messages, and (2) encoding the resulting matrix using Huffman encoding. Evaluation on three standard datasets demonstrates that this approach achieves accuracy comparable to other state-of-the-art methods but drastically cuts down processing time by approximately 98% and memory usage by around 96%.

This paper examines the Schreier growth within the context of actions by groups that are both solvable and of finite type. It demonstrates that for any such group $G$, there exists an integer $d$ such that the growth of the $n$-fold Schreier graph of $G$ relative to an l1-homomorphism from $G$ to the infinite cyclic group, with rank at most $G$'s dimension, is bounded by the function $O(n^d)$. This result implies two key theorems: first, that $G$ possesses a polynomial law of polynomial growth; secondly, that $G$ admits a series where each factor group has polynomial growth. These findings constitute significant steps toward resolving the longstanding Growth Conjecture for actions on trees, which asserts that any action of a finitely presented group having finite cohomological dimension on a tree has a finitely presented stabilizer.

Engineered to mimic animals, biological robots offer significant advantages due to their efficiency, agility, and ability to navigate complex environments. However, distinguishing them from inanimate objects remains difficult, as the primary mechanisms they emulate—muscle contraction and neural signaling—are challenging to physically detect. This study proposes a computational strategy to detect such internal signaling patterns in video footage. Initial results indicate that this method can effectively identify biology, including robotic forms emulating organic features, by analyzing subtle cues within video data.

Optimizing power network resource allocation is crucial for minimizing operational costs and addressing issues like network flow management. We propose utilizing quantum algorithms to optimize these power networks, demonstrating through case studies that such approaches outperform other methods when applied to both small and large-scale networks.

Machine learning offers significant advantages for extracting scientific knowledge from data, yet learning physical laws specifically remains a challenging task. We propose a novel, unsupervised approach that employs an autoencoder to represent data via a latent representation, subsequently applying symbolic regression on this representation to identify governing equations. The method's efficacy is validated through a series of tests involving multiple physics scenarios, demonstrating robust performance. The proposed framework was successfully used to derive equations for both the double pendulum and restricted three-body problem. Additionally, the approach can detect discrepancies in datasets, suggesting its potential utility for identifying modeling errors or flaws.

This study details a search for heavy, electrically charged new particles with masses exceeding 50 GeV/c² using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Analysis is based on a proton-proton collision dataset with an integrated luminosity of 36 fb⁻¹ collected at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The search targets particles that decay into nothing observable within the detector volume, manifesting as tracks with high ionisation energy loss. The analysis covers the expected signatures of theoretical frameworks involving charged particles with spin-0 or spin-1 resonances, as well as charged partners associated with supersymmetry. The results are expressed as 95% confidence level upper limits on the production cross-section, which are compared against predictions for standard model R-parity conserving supersymmetry. The findings indicate that charged gluinos with masses below 2.2 TeV/c² and electroweak partners (charginos and charged stops) with masses below 1.1 TeV/c² have been excluded. These observations align closely with previous exclusions derived from studies utilizing 12-TeV collision data.

This research presents near-unity efficiency in a ridge-waveguide quantum dot chip, achieving an extracted zero-detected coincidence rate ($\eta$) of $0.962 \pm 0.024$ as verified by $\chi^2$ analysis. Achieving this required growing self-assembled semiconductor quantum dots within the chip and performing precise etching to reach near-perfect ground-state resonance with the cavity. Under these optimal conditions, the system achieved a high extraction efficiency of $\eta_{ex} = 0.93 \pm 0.03$ alongside significant Purcell enhancement of $F_P = 8.4 \pm 1.4$ for the dot's emitter. Furthermore, the study achieved a state-of-the-art near-column source fidelity of $\eta_{src} = 0.987 \pm 0.003$ after laser tuning.

The boson peak, a feature in condensed matter physics first identified through dynamic mechanical analysis, refers to a prominent peak (often rounded) appearing in the plot of nonergodicity parameter versus frequency on a logarithmic scale. First identified using neutron scattering, it signifies a resonance in atomic vibrations occurring at frequencies far below those corresponding to a single bond's stiffness, a region previously difficult to probe. The current study reviews both theoretical and experimental evidence supporting the view that the boson peak stems from a resonance involving a self-affine network of soft bonds connected to a soft mode. This theoretical framework is consistent with experimental observations and offers a unified explanation for the phenomenon's nature.

Contemporary physics experiments demand high precision, especially as measurements approach fundamental limits set by current technology. In theoretical frameworks, this high accuracy necessaries state-of-the-art computational techniques for multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals. This paper presents an integrated strategy to compute such complex expressions numerically, combining cutting-edge graph analysis with various analytical and numerical methods. Graphical analysis is employed to identify the specific topological characteristics of these intricate diagrams that complicate standard integration approaches. We then convert the resulting momentum or loop-momentum expressions into Feynman parametric forms, facilitating evaluation through quadrature of the resulting functions. To manage singularities within these integrals, we apply feature-specific techniques including Feynman parametrization alongside sector decomposition. Finally, to achieve greater computational efficiency, we utilize multi-scale expansions to express outcomes as linear combinations of standard harmonic polylogarithms with specific coefficients. Throughout this discussion, we illustrate the practical application of our methodology using concrete examples drawn from high-precision Standard Model research.

Energy eigenchannels constitute a vital framework for analyzing wave scattering. This work establishes sum rules that characterize their contributions to energy depopulation. Specifically, we examine two categories of structures: fully open systems and fully mixed open-closed systems. For the former, we prove that every eigenchannel exists, with their depopulation rates governed by a set of sum rules. In systems that include open closed states, certain eigenchannels may be absent; however, the depopulation rates of both present and absent open-type eigenchannels are entirely specified by the same sum rules applied to their open closed counterparts. These findings are validated through explicit computations of eigenchannels in prototypical systems, including a double and triple open resonator and models representing molecular fluorescence.

The growing interest in the optimization of complex real-world systems has led to a rise in problems featuring multiple local optima that decision-makers need to explore for various reasons. This paper focuses on one of the primary drivers of such preference diversity: phenotypic diversity, which refers to the variety in the traits of organisms. We investigate how limited physical form variation constrains physical capabilities, causing multiple decision-makers to favor different solutions. Using an adaptive landscape search for navigation and solution evaluation, we examine these dynamics in environments both static and subject to changing conditions. We evaluate three methods: standard multi-objective optimization, a hybrid approach combining objective and environment diversity, and phenotype-based selection. Results indicate that while standard multi-objective methods yield superior local solutions, they fail to capture design diversity driven by distinct physical considerations. Conversely, focusing solely on phenotypic traits underestimates the impact of decision-makers with varying preferences. We find that accounting for both goals and environmental/physical variations provides the most effective strategy for preserving diverse designs.

The paper examines the multidimensional stable roommates task, extending the classic two-person stable roommates scenario to three. We establish that when individual preferences rely on three pairwise rankings and are governed by additive reasoning, the problem remains NP-complete. Furthermore, we introduce specific constraints that narrow the search to a restricted domain, proving that achieving stability is NP-hard within this setting as well.

We investigate how phonon-electron interactions influence valley physics in two-dimensional systems, specifically focusing on strain-induced electronic structures. In an ab initio framework, we examine strain-modified band arrangements for selected 2D materials—MoS₂, WS₂, and h-Bi₂Se₂—subsequently computing valley relaxation times via a rigorous many-body kernel that accounts for electron-phonon dynamics. Our findings reveal that relaxation mechanisms are heavily dependent on specific electronic structures; however, for the cases of MoS₂ and h-Bi₂Se₂, we identify similar valley lifetimes regardless of the underlying valley band arrangement. Additionally, we explore strain as a tool to engineer these relaxation times, achieving extensions of up to 100% in both MoS₂ and WS₂.

This work examines the class of metric spaces under the Gromov–Hausdorff distance that shares a fixed topological type homeomorphic to a given locally connected locally compact Hausdorff zero-set \(X_0\). We term such an collection a Gromov–Hausdorff cloud (or simply "cloud" for brevity). The primary finding establishes that for any set \(\mathcal{C}\) constituting a cloud, its GH-completion forms a metric space homeomorphic to \(X_0\), thereby confirming that every cloud is GH-completable. Furthermore, this completion possesses a unique "center," defined up to isometry within the sense of Z.-Li, whose significance and attributes are explored. The paper concludes by addressing various questions regarding centers within clouds.

The primary objective of decoders in fault-tolerant quantum computing is to determine the most probable error configuration from syndromes produced by a quantum error-correcting code. This study investigates employing reinforcement learning (RL) as a mechanism for training high-performance, generalizable neural network-based decoders. Our results demonstrate that RL-sourced neural networks can achieve performance comparable to leading existing decoding strategies. Furthermore, these trained networks offer the distinct advantage of being convertible into discrete systems, yielding policies that avoid the latency and processing time typically associated with traditional belief propagation or maximum likelihood decoding methods.

Quantum metrology leverages the principles of quantum mechanics to enhance measurement precision beyond classical limits. This contribution demonstrates its application in determining a coupling-strength parameter through quantum jump metrology involving a two-cavity network. We compare two approaches: a standard strategy employing pure quantum states and a quantum super-radiance strategy utilizing an entangled state. In both scenarios, we demonstrate that increasing the coupling between the two cavities yields improved accuracy. When using a coherent state, the error probability follows a quadratic scaling with the probability of quantum jumps; the ent超辐射 strategy further lowers this floor, establishing a distinct advantage over coherent-state-based methods. Ultimately, we show that both schemes achieve precision exceeding classical metrological bounds, with the ent超辐射 method representing the pinnacle of performance among the examined techniques.

The PHENIX collaboration reports findings on direct photon-hadron correlations in collisions involving d+Au, C+Cu, and Au+Au at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV. In photon-jet asymmetry analyses, these photons serve as calibrated probes for the associated hadron jets. The data indicate that in d+Au events, the hadron-jet correlation functions align with vacuum fragmentation expectations, whereas C+Cu and Au+Au systems exhibit suppression in the forward direction relative to fragmentation, consistent with findings from earlier experiments. Furthermore, hadron-jet correlation functions in Au+Au collisions are utilized to quantify the modification of the hadron spectra within the medium.

We investigate an analog-digitalhybrid framework in quantum computing that enables any quantum algorithm to run with just one quantum circuit featuring alternating long and short gate operations. As a testbed for this approach, we examine fermionic systems, beginning with $1D$ spinless fermions on which we run digitized versions of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and the Hubbard model to demonstrate its viability. Additionally, we run evolved Heisenberg feromonics on a $2D$ lattice to show that this method works effectively in higher dimensions as well.

Although deep neural networks are celebrated for their ability to automatically extract relevant features, a critical issue remains: which specific features truly drive optimal performance? This paper introduces a method to enhance representation learning by jointly addressing two objectives: (1) improving generalization and (2) explicitly learning features that aid generalization. We address the first goal using standard techniques and the second by integrating Rich Feature Construction (RFC), which optimizes an optimization-generalization dilemma (OGD). This approach seeks to maximize the synergy between distinct architectural components, ensuring that interdependencies in feature interactions support the generalization of other elements. Consequently, maximizing RFC objectives creates incentives for the network to discover high-generalization features. Empirical results across various tasks demonstrate that integrating RFC with a given model architecture not only improves overall performance but also successfully identifies the most beneficial features for generalizing to unseen data.

Creating 3D microstructures within biological tissues is vital for basic biological research and medical diagnostics. While optical methods are highly effective for this purpose, current techniques struggle to generate multiple complex shapes concurrently. This study introduces a new approach utilizing a hybrid system of vector space decomposition and phase-only spatial light modulation combined with a fluence limitation technique (FLC-SLM). This method offers a computationally efficient algorithm capable of shaping arbitrary complex tissues with superior precision and flexibility compared to existing 3D optical writing methods.

We express our gratitude for the thorough review offered by the three editors and the three dedicated reviewers. Their insightful comments and constructive criticisms have been extremely valuable to us. In this response, addressed to each query raised by the reviewers, we outline the modifications we have made to address the concerns raised.

Monolithic CMOS sensors utilizing the small collection-electrode design feature fixed, minimally scaled pixelated anodes integrated within a standard CMOS n-well. This architecture enables n-wens to function as sensors with quasi-uniform electric fields, a feature supported by simulations demonstrating that sensor thickness critically influences the near-field near-field distribution. Consequently, sensor thickness becomes a pivotal factor affecting the near-field distribution. This factor significantly impacts the near-field distribution, making its optimization essential. To address this, we present CLICTD, a technology demonstrator featuring 300×300 n-well sensors fabricated across various thicknesses and two distinct substrate materials: silicon and sapphire. We offer an experimental measurement of the near-field distribution by comparing near-field distributions measured experimentally and simulated under different operating voltages. Comparisons between sapphire and silicon substrates are also provided to evaluate the impact of material differences on the near-field distribution.

We describe the initial experimental deployment of the rapid atmospheric self-coherence imagery technique for adaptive optical correction, implemented on the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optical Laboratory testbed in San Francisco. This system uniquely integrates three components: an extreme adaptive optical mirror with approximately 500× more sampling than standard configurations, a high-speed focal plane wavefront sensor (FSFWS) capable of detecting atmospheric turbulence residuals, and a conventional adaptive optical subsystem. During the experiment, the FSFWS operated at approximately 4,000 Hz to gather coherence maps, driving an independent adaptive loop running at roughly 2,500 Hz. This loop modified wavefront errors specifically attributed to atmospheric speckles, complementing the main atmospheric loop. The results show that the dual-loop strategy enhanced angular resolution and significantly diminished residual atmospheric and turbulence-related noise.

This study examines a shifted Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) interest rate model enhanced with a deterministic shift factor. The model is developed to address negative interest rates while maintaining analytical tractability. By applying an implicit equation, we link these rates to long-term yields and construct a compatible positive interest rate structure. In this framework, we derive an implicit formula for the equivalent positive term spread. Furthermore, we analyze the statistical properties of a spread portfolio and, for the deterministically shifted Model, provide an implicit formula for its value.

Active experiments like DUNE are designed to investigate neutrino oscillations in the presence of sterile states. We analyze DUNE's capacity to detect sterile neutrinos within the energy range of $1$ to $6\,\mathrm{GeV}$, focusing on two primary strategies.

The first approach examines the disappearance of an $\nu_\mu$ beam traveling over long distances. We assess the sensitivity of this technique for various mass scales, accounting for uncertainties inherent in the low-energy $\nu_\mu$ cross-sections.

The second approach investigates active–sterile mixing using an off-axis $\nu_\mu$ source. In this scenario, we analyze the reconstructed energy spectrum of detected events to identify deviations caused by sterile states, specifically looking for regions where the oscillation probability is suppressed.

Our findings indicate that combining these methodologies allows DUNE to probe sterile states with masses in the range of $0.1$ to $1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ with significant sensitivity, even in the presence of substantial nuclear model uncertainties.

Meta-analyses frequently involve studies that evaluate multiple interventions, creating natural clusters. In such contexts, cluster-robust variance estimators (CRREs) are the preferred method for calculating confidence intervals. This paper introduces a novel, computationally efficient CRRE for the mixed-effects model, designed specifically for data structures where multiple interventions are assessed per trial. We evaluate the performance of our proposed estimator against the standard approach using the `metafor` package, particularly in the presence of multivariate meta-regression. Through comprehensive simulations and a real-world dataset, we demonstrate that the new estimator offers a substantial performance advantage over existing methods, especially when multivariate modeling is applied.

This work introduces a multi-time-step algorithm designed to enhance computational efficiency in particle-resolved simulations involving binary collisions. It merges multiple integrators, each tailored to specific sub-time-steps, and synchronizes them using Altschul's adaptive time-rescaling technique. This approach accounts for physical time scales to manage algal interactions accurately. Collision handling employs ALAS (Adaptive Local Sub-steps), where individual particles utilize optimized integrators based on their characteristic interaction times, further reduced by a global adaptive step. Resolved to various accuracy levels, this strategy successfully improves computational performance for particle-resolved simulations while maintaining high numerical precision.

This study examines the energy origin of radiation in the Unruh and Hawking effects, with a focus on defining particle count based on conservation laws. The findings indicate that particle emission stems from disparities in how different observers define particle number due to conservation laws, rather than gravitational-force-induced pair creation.
